UNIT 2 / WEEK 1 / CHAPTER 1

Relational database foundations

Find out what a school equipment desk needs to know, then use its loan records to answer a question. You will compare a simple register with related database tables.

DATA MANAGEMENT CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Distinguish data from information in a stated context.
  • Compare a flat-file approach with a relational design.
  • Distinguish a database from a DBMS and an RDBMS.
  • Explain data independence and the role of software in managing access.

Before you start: No earlier database lesson is required. Use the supplied fictional records.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads · Practice after reading: Model records before querying.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Start with a question

Imagine you run the school equipment desk. You need to know which items are still on loan and which are overdue.

Your register stores a loan identifier, borrower identifier, item identifier, due date and return status. These stored values are data. When you use them to answer a question, the answer is information.

“2026-04-06” alone does not say whether an item is overdue: we also need today’s date and whether it has been returned. For this activity, assume today is 8 April 2026, regardless of the real date. An overdue loan is unreturned and has a due date strictly before today. An item due today is not overdue under this rule.

Requirements determine the rule. A different school might define a time-of-day deadline, so clarify the requirement before building a report.

2. Inspect the flat-file starter

A flat file stores records in a single tabular structure. Our CSV has one row per loan and one header row naming its fields. CSV is a text format; it does not by itself enforce database relationships or permissions. Opening it in a spreadsheet does not automatically make it a relational database.

LoanIDBorrowerIDBorrowerLabelEquipmentIDEquipmentDescriptionDueDateReturned
L001B001Learner AE01Camera2026-04-06False
L002B002Learner BE02Tripod2026-04-08False
L003B001Learner AE03Recorder2026-04-07True
L004B003Learner CE04Camera2026-04-10False
L005B002Learner BE02Tripod2026-04-04True
L006B004Learner DE05Microphone2026-04-07False

All borrower labels are synthetic. True and False in the CSV are text representations of return status; imported data needs conversion according to the chosen database’s types. Dates use year-month-day notation.

Six rows represent six loans. E02 appears twice because an item can have a history of loans. Those two loans have different LoanIDs and return statuses. B001 appears twice because a borrower can borrow more than one item. Do not delete repeated identifiers without checking what the rows represent.

Download synthetic loan data

3. Turn records into information

Use the reporting date of 8 April 2026 and work through two checks:

  1. Remove returned loans from the result. L001, L002, L004 and L006 remain: four items are on loan.
  2. Check which remaining due dates are strictly before 8 April. L001 and L006 qualify: two loans are overdue.
RecordReturned?Due before today?Overdue?
L001NoYesYes
L002NoNo: due todayNo
L003YesYesNo
L006NoYesYes

The conclusion “two overdue loans” is information for a stated date and rule. It is only as reliable as the recorded dates and return statuses. A valid-looking date can still be factually wrong.

Visual walkthrough

Which loans are overdue?

Apply the two checks to a loan. Use 8 April 2026 as the reporting date.

Pause and predict: Why is L003 excluded even though 7 April is before the reporting date?

Show the explanation

It has already been returned. An earlier due date alone does not make it overdue.

Try a small change: Move the reporting date to 9 April. Explain why L002 now qualifies, assuming it is still unreturned.

4. Why separate related facts?

Try changing Learner B’s label in the flat register. You must edit both L002 and L005. If you change only one, the same BorrowerID has conflicting labels.

Deletion can lose facts too. If you remove E05’s final loan, you also remove this register’s only description of that item. These problems grow as you repeat more facts.

A relational design can store different kinds of facts in related tables. A Borrower table stores each borrower’s details. Equipment stores each item’s details. Loan stores each borrowing event and references the borrower and item through identifiers. Later chapters define keys, relationships and normalisation formally.

Borrower: whoLoan: borrowing eventEquipment: which item

In this starter, the three sets contain four borrower records, five equipment records and six loan records. A loan still needs its own identifier because a borrower can borrow the same item again at a later time. This is a conceptual introduction, not the final four-table project design.

Separate tables reduce duplication when designed well; they do not automatically eliminate mistakes. Incorrect links, weak constraints or poorly designed tables can still produce unreliable results.

5. Database, DBMS and RDBMS

Keep the stored records separate in your mind from the software that manages them. The equipment desk’s organised loan records form a database.

A database management system (DBMS) is the software you use to define, store, retrieve and change those records. A relational DBMS (RDBMS) manages data using related tables.

A user or application asks the DBMS to perform an operation. The DBMS interprets the request, checks configured rules and accesses storage. Appropriate systems can manage permissions, constraints and concurrent operations; the exact facilities depend on the product and configuration. It is not enough to own a DBMS: controls must be set up and used correctly.

For our desk, a learner might view equipment availability while authorised staff record returns. A read-only report should not provide unrestricted editing. We will explore permissions and security more deeply later in Unit 2.

One physical file does not mean flat-file organisation. SQLite can store several related tables inside a single database file. “Flat” describes the logical organisation, not how many files you see in a folder. SQLite also relies on application and operating-system controls for access; do not assume every RDBMS has server-style user accounts.

Technical references: PostgreSQL relational concepts and SQLite architecture.

6. What does data independence mean?

Suppose you add an index to help the DBMS find loans faster. Your report can still request LoanID and DueDate without knowing where their bytes are stored.

This separation is an example of physical data independence: you can change aspects of storage without rewriting the application’s request. It also helps several tools use the same managed records.

Independence is not absolute compatibility. Renaming a column used by a report can require changes to that report. Moving to another DBMS may require data conversion and query changes. A backup or export remains valuable, but copying a database file does not mean every other DBMS can read it directly.

For the equipment desk, keep the data definition, business rules and storage separate from the screen layout. A new screen should not need a second inconsistent copy of borrower records.

7. Choose an approach for the requirement

RequirementReasoned choice
One small temporary list, one editor, simple exchangeA CSV may be sufficient if checking and access are manageable.
Borrower and equipment details reused across a growing loan historyRelated tables help maintain those facts separately.
Several users editing simultaneously with different permissionsChoose and configure a system supporting the required concurrency and access controls.

Justify the choice against the requirements, maintenance burden and risks. “Databases are always better” is not an explanation.

Practice and explain

Interpret

Why is L003 not overdue even though its due date is before 8 April?

Show explained answer

Its Returned status is True. The overdue rule requires both an earlier due date and an unreturned loan.

Distinguish

Is a printed “two overdue loans” report the same thing as the raw records?

Show explained answer

No. It is an interpretation derived from records using a stated date and rule. The raw values support the conclusion.

Diagnose

A classmate removes L005 because E02 already appears in L002. Why is that a mistake?

Show explained answer

The rows describe different borrowing events. Repeated equipment identifiers can be legitimate history; LoanID distinguishes the loans.

Explain

A database containing three related tables is stored in one SQLite file. Is it a flat-file register?

Show explained answer

No. Its logical structure is relational even though its physical storage uses one file.

Evaluate

Does a DBMS having access-control features mean every user is automatically restricted?

Show explained answer

No. Appropriate permissions and application/operating-system controls must be configured; facilities differ by system.

Your practical task

Using the CSV and workbook, count active and overdue loans for 8 April 2026, explain repeated facts, propose Borrower/Equipment/Loan responsibilities and justify who should be able to view or edit the records. State one limitation of your analysis.

Show illustrative answer / example

Four active loans: L001, L002, L004, L006. Two overdue: L001, L006. Borrower holds four distinct borrowers; Equipment five distinct items; Loan six events referring to both. Repeated labels/descriptions create inconsistent-update risk in the flat register. Staff may edit authorised loan records; learners may view permitted availability. The counts rely on truthful and current return status, the supplied date and the defined boundary rule.

Check your understanding

Which statement is correct?

One physical file always means flat-file data An RDBMS manages relational data; several tables can share a physical file A report is reliable even when return status is wrong

Quick-check answer and explanation

An RDBMS manages relational data; several tables can share a physical file

Distinguish logical organisation from physical storage. The RDBMS manages data, while report reliability still depends on valid rules and accurate records.

Chapter recap

Data are stored values; information answers a question using those values and a rule. Related tables give different facts a clear home. A database holds the data; the DBMS manages it. Data independence allows some changes without rewriting applications, but it does not guarantee compatibility.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: introduce the equipment desk; distinguish raw values from an answer and state the overdue rule. Evidence: identify needed fields and calculate active/overdue counts.
  2. Lesson 2: inspect the flat register; simulate changing one repeated label and deleting an item’s last loan. Evidence: explain the maintenance problem.
  3. Lesson 3: distinguish database/DBMS/RDBMS; sort facts into Borrower, Equipment and Loan; discuss independence and configured access. Evidence: a labelled concept sketch and two explanations.
  4. Lesson 4: complete the workbook independently, compare explained answers, then answer a new boundary case. Evidence: corrections and an exit justification. Four lessons total, with optional practice and explained answers.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 2 / CHAPTER 2

Modelling entities and relationships

Decide what each table should store before you build it. You will identify borrowers, equipment and loan events, then connect them with keys and clear relationship rules.

DATABASE DESIGN CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Distinguish entity types, attributes, records and fields.
  • Choose and justify primary, foreign and composite keys.
  • Explain one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships.
  • Read and create a four-table crow’s-foot ER diagram and a data dictionary.

Before you start: Distinguish a table, a record and a field.

Revisit if needed: Relational database foundations.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. From entity to table

Start by asking what you need to keep facts about. At the equipment desk, you need borrowers, equipment items and loan events.

An entity is one distinguishable thing or event. Learner A, equipment item E01 and loan L001 are examples. An entity type groups similar entities: Borrower, Equipment and Loan are the types in this model.

An attribute is a property you record, such as a borrower’s label or a loan’s due date.

In a relational implementation, a table represents an entity type, a row (record) represents an instance, and a column (field) represents an attribute. A single field value belongs to a row: L001’s DueDate is 2026-04-06. Distinguish the column definition from that particular stored value.

Loan is an event entity. Keeping events separately preserves history without repeatedly storing borrower labels and equipment descriptions.

2. Choose identifiers deliberately

Ask how you will distinguish two records even when their descriptions match. E01 and E04 are both cameras, so EquipmentDescription cannot identify an item uniquely.

Consider every set of fields that could uniquely identify a row under your rules. Remove any field that is unnecessary for uniqueness. What remains is a candidate key.

Choose one candidate key as the primary key. It may contain one field or several. A small sample with no repeated values does not prove that a field will always be unique.

A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row under the agreed rules: no attribute can be removed without losing uniqueness. The design chooses one candidate key as the primary key. A key may contain several columns. Never infer a permanent uniqueness rule from a small sample that happens to have no duplicate values.

A foreign key references a permitted key in another table (or the same table). In this model Loan.BorrowerID references Borrower.BorrowerID. Foreign-key values can repeat: B001 appears in L001 and L003. An FK is not automatically the primary key of its table.

Our foreign keys are required, so every loan must reference an existing borrower and item. Elsewhere an optional relationship might allow a null foreign key if the design permits it. Appropriate database constraints enforce these choices when implemented.

We retain all six loan events from the foundations CSV. The new Category table groups item types. The category assignments are an explicit new design decision: cameras are Imaging, tripods Support, and recorders/microphones Audio. Categories can exist before items are registered.

Show the explanation

4. Read relationships in both directions

RelationshipRule from the parentRule from the child
Borrower–LoanA borrower can have zero or many loansA loan has exactly one borrower
Equipment–LoanAn item can have zero or many loans over timeA loan refers to exactly one item
Category–EquipmentA category can contain zero or many itemsAn item belongs to exactly one category

Read each relationship twice: once from the parent to its children, then from a child back to its parent. One borrower can have many loans, but each loan refers to one borrower. This is a one-to-many relationship; the foreign key is stored on the many side.

  • Minimum participation tells you whether zero instances are allowed or at least one is required.
  • Maximum participation tells you whether the upper limit is one or many.

Read the symbols at an end as the number of instances at that end for one instance at the other end.

One-to-one example: if each assigned locker can belong to at most one borrower and each borrower can have at most one locker, the maximum is one in both directions. Whether every borrower must have a locker is a separate rule. A unique foreign key plus appropriate nullability may be part of the implementation.

Many-to-many example: over time, one borrower uses many items and one item is used by many borrowers. Loan resolves this into two one-to-many relationships and stores event facts. This does not mean one physical item is available for two active loans at once. That additional business rule needs checking beyond basic foreign keys.

5. Draw and interpret crow’s-foot notation

Two bars mean exactly one. A circle with a crow’s foot means zero or many. Read Category to Equipment: each item has exactly one category, while a category can have zero or many items. Explain all three connections aloud, then redraw the diagram without copying the image.

Download the worked SVG diagram. Compare your notation with the SCSA support booklet, printed page 15. Table positions and line bends are layout choices; keys and relationship rules determine meaning.

6. When a composite key fits

A composite key uses two or more attributes together. Suppose WorkshopEnrolment records a borrower in a workshop, with one enrolment allowed per borrower/workshop pair. The pair (BorrowerID, WorkshopID) can be its primary key. Both fields also reference their parent tables.

BorrowerID (PK, FK)WorkshopID (PK, FK)
B001W01
B001W02
B002W01

Repeating B001 or W01 individually is allowed; repeating the same pair is not. These are example extension records, not part of the four-table equipment dataset.

Do not use (BorrowerID, EquipmentID) alone as Loan’s key. A borrower can borrow the same item again, so the pair can legitimately repeat across events. Our LoanID identifies each event. Adding dates to a proposed key requires explicit rules about whether the resulting combination is always unique.

7. Document the fields and their rules

Before you implement the tables, write down what each field means and what values it allows. This record of field definitions is a data dictionary.

For each field, record its name, type, size, meaning and constraints. Here, text sizes are maximum character lengths chosen for the exercise. Date and Boolean storage sizes depend on the DBMS.

A default of False applies to a new loan when no return status is supplied. It does not change the status of historical loans.

ElementConceptual typeSizeDescriptionConstraints
Borrower.BorrowerIDText4Synthetic borrower identifierPK; unique; required; B + three digits
Borrower.BorrowerLabelText40Display labelRequired; not assumed unique
Category.CategoryIDText3Equipment category identifierPK; unique; required; C + two digits
Category.CategoryNameText30Category labelRequired; unique by our agreed rule
Equipment.EquipmentIDText3Physical item identifierPK; unique; required; E + two digits
Equipment.EquipmentDescriptionText60Item descriptionRequired; may repeat
Equipment.CategoryIDText3Category of the itemRequired FK → Category.CategoryID
Loan.LoanIDText4Borrowing event identifierPK; unique; required; L + three digits
Loan.BorrowerIDText4Borrower for this eventRequired FK → Borrower.BorrowerID
Loan.EquipmentIDText3Item for this eventRequired FK → Equipment.EquipmentID
Loan.DueDateDateDBMS-definedDue dateRequired; displayed as YYYY-MM-DD
Loan.ReturnedBooleanDBMS-definedReturn statusRequired; default False for a new loan

Identifiers are text because the letters and leading zeros matter. Use integer for a count, float for an approximate measurement such as item mass, Boolean for return status, text for a label and date for a due date. The conceptual types must later be mapped to the selected DBMS. SQLite, for example, has different storage/type behaviour from a database with a native DATE type.

Formats and lengths are design decisions, not universal rules. A future identifier range beyond E99 would require a revised specification. Validation confirms format and allowed links, not that the stored fact is truthful.

8. Check the design against counterexamples

  • Two borrowers share a display label: their identifiers must still distinguish them.
  • B001 borrows E01 again: add a new LoanID, rather than overwriting L001.
  • A loan refers to B999, which does not exist: reject the required reference.
  • Category C04 has no items yet: the optional-many rule permits that category.
  • Someone deletes Borrower B001 while loans still refer to it: choose a deliberate deletion policy. For this learning model, restrict deletion until references are resolved; do not silently destroy history.

Review the intended rules, keys and sample data together. A plausible drawing is insufficient if it cannot store legitimate events or prevent invalid references.

9. Model pack and independent practice

Download student workbook Download explained answers

Download the four related datasets: Borrower, Category, Equipment, Loan. Keep synthetic records for this exercise. SQL setup is not required.

10. Resolve update, insertion and deletion anomalies with evidence

Begin with business dependencies, not a rule that every repeated value is wrong. In the supplied flat membership table the key is (StudentID, ClubID). StudentID determines StudentName; ClubID determines ClubName and CoachID; CoachID determines CoachPhone. Each student may join many clubs, each club may have many students, and each club currently has one coach.

AnomalyFlat-table problemResolution and check
UpdateChanging T1's phone in only one membership leaves conflicting copiesUpdate one Coach row; all related clubs obtain that phone through a join
InsertionA new club with no members cannot be represented without inventing a student or breaking the membership keyInsert the Club independently, then add Membership rows when students join
DeletionDeleting the last Film membership loses Film's club/coach facts from the flat tableDelete the Membership only; Club and Coach records remain

The rows already have atomic values, so they can be in 1NF while still having anomalies. To reach 2NF for this composite-key design, separate Student and Club facts from Membership because they depend on only part of the key. At that stage Club may still store CoachPhone. To reach 3NF, separate Coach because ClubID determines CoachID which determines CoachPhone. The final relations are Student, Coach, Club and Membership. Keep linking keys and enforce relationships so decomposition does not disconnect facts.

Reconstruct the original memberships with a join before the independent insert/update/delete activities, checking both missing and extra rows. The fixture's repeated facts are consistent; real conflicting records require investigation. SELECT DISTINCT can suppress identical projections but cannot decide which conflicting phone number is true. A repeated foreign key is expected in a one-to-many relationship and is not by itself a normalisation error.

Pause and predict

If the final Film membership is deleted in the flat table, which facts disappear? Should deleting a membership mean the club no longer exists?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download anomalies_lab.sql

-- Fresh disposable SQLite database. Fixture dependencies are explicitly stated.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE FlatMembership (
    StudentID TEXT, StudentName TEXT, ClubID TEXT, ClubName TEXT,
    CoachID TEXT, CoachPhone TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
INSERT INTO FlatMembership VALUES
('S1', 'Ari', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S2', 'Bo', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S1', 'Ari', 'C2', 'Film', 'T2', '201');
CREATE TABLE Student (StudentID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, StudentName TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Coach (CoachID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, CoachPhone TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Club (
    ClubID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ClubName TEXT NOT NULL,
    CoachID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Coach(CoachID)
);
CREATE TABLE Membership (
    StudentID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(StudentID),
    ClubID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Club(ClubID),
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
-- DISTINCT copies known-consistent fixture facts; it does not resolve conflicts.
INSERT INTO Student SELECT DISTINCT StudentID, StudentName FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Coach SELECT DISTINCT CoachID, CoachPhone FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Club SELECT DISTINCT ClubID, ClubName, CoachID FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Membership SELECT StudentID, ClubID FROM FlatMembership;
-- Capture a reconstruction before the independent modification activities.
CREATE TABLE ReconstructedBefore AS
SELECT s.StudentID, s.StudentName, c.ClubID, c.ClubName, t.CoachID, t.CoachPhone
FROM Membership AS m
JOIN Student AS s ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
JOIN Club AS c ON c.ClubID = m.ClubID
JOIN Coach AS t ON t.CoachID = c.CoachID;
UPDATE Coach SET CoachPhone = '299' WHERE CoachID = 'T1';
INSERT INTO Club VALUES ('C3', 'Coding', 'T1');
DELETE FROM Membership WHERE StudentID = 'S1' AND ClubID = 'C2';
SELECT ClubID, ClubName FROM Club ORDER BY ClubID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Draw arrows for each stated dependency. Complete the 1NF → 2NF → 3NF table splits, keeping keys visible. Predict a join that reconstructs each original membership exactly once.
  2. Independent transfer: Use the SQL fixture to add Coding with no members, update T1's phone once, and remove Film's last membership. Verify the club and coach survive. Transfer to Asset(AssetID, AssetName, RoomID, RoomName), where each RoomID determines one RoomName.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Given a new scenario, name the dependency causing each anomaly before proposing a split. Explain why atomic fields alone do not establish 3NF.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Club relation retains C1 Robotics, C2 Film and C3 Coding. C2 has no memberships but still exists. T1's phone becomes 299 in one Coach row. The asset transfer splits Room(RoomID PK, RoomName) and Asset(AssetID PK, AssetName, RoomID FK). Prove the relationships preserve the intended facts; do not delete repeated foreign keys.

Practice and explain

Choose

Why is EquipmentDescription not a suitable primary key?

Show explained answer

Descriptions can repeat: both E01 and E04 are Camera. A key must identify each item, not merely its type.

Trace

Which fields link L003 to its borrower and category?

Show explained answer

Loan.BorrowerID B001 links to Borrower B001. Loan.EquipmentID E03 links to Equipment E03, whose CategoryID C03 links to Audio.

Explain

May BorrowerID repeat in Loan?

Show explained answer

Yes. It is a foreign key there, and a borrower can have several loan events. LoanID remains unique.

Challenge

Can the pair B001/E01 identify every future loan?

Show explained answer

No. The same borrower can borrow that item again. A new loan event needs its own identifier or a justified larger unique key.

Read

Does a category with zero equipment violate this diagram?

Show explained answer

No. Category to Equipment is optional many, so zero items are permitted. Each existing item still requires one category.

Your practical task

Redraw the four-table ER diagram, underline PKs and label FKs. Explain each relationship in both directions, reproduce a data dictionary for Loan, then add a second B001/E01 event with a new LoanID. Explain which rules a duplicate LoanID and a B999 reference violate.

Show illustrative answer / example

Use Borrower.BorrowerID, Category.CategoryID, Equipment.EquipmentID and Loan.LoanID as primary keys. Equipment.CategoryID and Loan.BorrowerID/EquipmentID are required foreign keys. Each parent permits zero or many children; each child requires exactly one referenced parent. A new loan such as L007/B001/E01 is a distinct event with its own due date/status. Duplicate L001 violates key uniqueness; B999 violates the required valid-borrower reference. A second simultaneous active loan for E01 would require a separate business-rule check.

Check your understanding

Which key fits Loan when the same borrower can borrow the same item again?

BorrowerLabel BorrowerID + EquipmentID alone A unique LoanID for each borrowing event

Quick-check answer and explanation

A unique LoanID for each borrowing event

A borrowing pair can repeat over time. LoanID distinguishes the event; borrower and item identifiers are foreign keys.

Chapter recap

Use a key to identify each record and a foreign key to link related records. Read relationships in both directions and state whether participation is optional or required. A diagram shows the structure; a data dictionary explains the fields. Test both against examples that could break your rules.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: retrieve the flat-register problems; distinguish entities, instances, fields and records; choose identifiers. Evidence: annotated table definitions.
  2. Lesson 2: locate primary/foreign keys in the four datasets; test repeat events and invalid references; compare composite keys. Evidence: justified key choices.
  3. Lesson 3: read relationships in both directions and model minimum/maximum participation; redraw the crow’s-foot diagram. Evidence: a four-table ER diagram and spoken explanations.
  4. Lesson 4: complete the Loan data dictionary and independent workbook; review counterexamples and corrections. Evidence: diagram/dictionary revisions. Four lessons total, with optional practice and explained answers.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 3 / CHAPTER 3

Normalisation

Find out why repeated facts make a register hard to maintain. You will reorganise reservation records into related tables while keeping every original event. This process is called normalisation.

DATABASE DESIGN CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Recognise insert, update and delete anomalies.
  • Flatten repeating groups into 1NF with justified keys.
  • Remove partial dependencies for 2NF and transitive dependencies for 3NF.
  • Check that the decomposition preserves the original facts.

Before you start: Identify primary keys, foreign keys and relationships.

Revisit if needed: Modelling entities and relationships.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. State the rules before choosing a key

The equipment desk accepts reservation requests as well as recording loans. A reservation is a request for a particular item on a particular date; it is not an issued loan. Competing requests from different borrowers may exist for the same item/date. At most one request is recorded for a given borrower, item and date.

The composite key is therefore (BorrowerID, EquipmentID, ReservationDate). One borrower can request an item again on another date. BorrowerID alone, EquipmentID alone, or borrower/item alone cannot identify every reservation.

ReservationStatus is Requested or Confirmed in this exercise. Approval and availability rules must be checked separately; normalisation alone does not stop conflicting bookings. The earlier Loan model continues to use LoanID for each single-item borrowing event.

2. Start with a repeating group

A clerk keeps one row per borrower with several reservation details inside one cell. Another version might use Item1, Date1, Item2, Date2 and so on. Both approaches make the number of reservations part of the record layout.

BorrowerIDBorrowerLabelReservations stored together
B001Learner AE01 / 2026-05-01 / Confirmed; E02 / 2026-05-01 / Requested; E01 / 2026-05-08 / Requested
B002Learner BE01 / 2026-05-02 / Confirmed; E01 / 2026-05-01 / Requested
B003Learner CE03 / 2026-05-02 / Confirmed

The downloadable JSON also contains each item’s description and category. Its nested reservations are a teaching representation of the repeating group, not a claim that JSON itself is invalid or unsuitable for all applications.

Give each reservation its own row and each field one value for its defined purpose. This is the change you need for a relational table in first normal form.

One value does not mean one character. “Learner A” can stay together as a label. Whether a value is atomic depends on what the attribute means and how you use it.

3. Recognise the anomalies

Update: E01’s description appears in several reservation entries. Editing only one leaves conflicting descriptions for the same item.

Insert: the register cannot naturally store a new equipment item with no reservation because its rows require reservation key values. Inventing a borrower or date would record a false event.

Delete: removing the only reservation for E03 loses this register’s only stored description of that recorder and its category.

These problems concern how facts depend on identifiers. A real duplicate event is different from a legitimately repeated equipment identifier. Deleting repeated IDs blindly can destroy history.

4. 1NF: one reservation per row

Flatten the repeating group into six rows with the same named fields, one value per field and no repeating column groups. Identify each reservation using the stated composite key. Underline all three components, not just the first.

ReservationRegister (BorrowerID, EquipmentID, ReservationDate, BorrowerLabel, EquipmentDescription, CategoryID, CategoryName, ReservationStatus)

BorrowerIDBorrowerLabelEquipmentIDEquipmentDescriptionCategoryIDCategoryNameReservationDateReservationStatus
B001Learner AE01CameraC01Imaging2026-05-01Confirmed
B001Learner AE02TripodC02Support2026-05-01Requested
B002Learner BE01CameraC01Imaging2026-05-02Confirmed
B001Learner AE01CameraC01Imaging2026-05-08Requested
B003Learner CE03RecorderC03Audio2026-05-02Confirmed
B002Learner BE01CameraC01Imaging2026-05-01Requested

B001/E01 occurs on both 1 May and 8 May. B001/E01/1 May and B002/E01/1 May are separate requests. These examples show why all three key components matter under our rules. The table is in 1NF, but duplicated descriptive facts still create anomalies.

Read the notation: ReservationRegister is the table name. The names inside its brackets are fields, not stored values. The underlined fields together form the primary key. You need all three because B001 can request E01 again on a different date.

5. Dependencies explain the next split

Ask: if you know one value, which other values should it determine? If you know BorrowerID, you should be able to find that borrower’s label.

This rule is a functional dependency, written X → Y: one value of X determines one value of Y. It describes a data rule, not a physical cause.

Use the requirements to decide dependencies. Sample data can reveal a broken rule, but a small sample cannot prove that a rule will always hold.

BorrowerID → BorrowerLabel
EquipmentID → EquipmentDescription, CategoryID
CategoryID → CategoryName
(BorrowerID, EquipmentID, ReservationDate) → ReservationStatus

BorrowerLabel depends on BorrowerID, only part of the composite reservation key. Equipment details depend on EquipmentID, another part. Those are partial dependencies. Status can vary between borrowers, items and dates, so it belongs to the whole reservation event.

EquipmentID determines CategoryID, which determines CategoryName. CategoryName therefore has a transitive dependency through a non-key attribute. We address that after removing partial dependencies.

Try the key test: cover EquipmentID and ReservationDate. Knowing B001 still tells you the borrower label, Learner A, so BorrowerLabel depends on only part of the reservation key. Now try to find ReservationStatus from B001 alone: you cannot, because that borrower has several requests. You need the complete borrower/item/date combination.

Visual walkthrough

Which key does each fact depend on?

The reservation key is BorrowerID + EquipmentID + ReservationDate.

Pause and predict: Why does BorrowerLabel move out of Reservation when you form 2NF?

Show the explanation

It depends on BorrowerID alone, not on the complete three-part key. Borrower gives that fact its own home.

Try a small change: Explain why ReservationStatus stays with the complete reservation key.

6. 2NF: remove partial dependencies

Give facts that depend on only part of the reservation key their own tables:

  1. Move BorrowerLabel to Borrower, keyed by BorrowerID.
  2. Move the item’s descriptive facts to Equipment, keyed by EquipmentID.
  3. Keep the three-part key and ReservationStatus in Reservation. BorrowerID and EquipmentID also become foreign keys.

You have removed partial dependencies: non-key facts no longer depend on only part of this composite key.

Borrower (BorrowerID, BorrowerLabel)

Equipment (EquipmentID, EquipmentDescription, CategoryID, CategoryName)

Reservation (BorrowerID FK, EquipmentID FK, ReservationDate, ReservationStatus)

BorrowerIDBorrowerLabel
B001Learner A
B002Learner B
B003Learner C
EquipmentIDEquipmentDescriptionCategoryIDCategoryName
E01CameraC01Imaging
E02TripodC02Support
E03RecorderC03Audio
BorrowerIDEquipmentIDReservationDateReservationStatus
B001E012026-05-01Confirmed
B001E012026-05-08Requested
B001E022026-05-01Requested
B002E012026-05-01Requested
B002E012026-05-02Confirmed
B003E032026-05-02Confirmed

There are three borrowers, three items and six reservations. Descriptions now occur once per equipment item. ReservationStatus depends on the whole reservation key. CategoryName still depends on CategoryID inside Equipment, so a transitive dependency remains.

For the straightforward keys used here, a 1NF table with a single-attribute key has no partial dependency on part of that key. It can still have transitive dependencies and fail 3NF. Simply adding an ID column does not automatically solve every dependency problem.

Why Category stays for now: at this step you remove facts that depend on only part of the reservation key. EquipmentID determines the item details, so they move together to Equipment. Inside Equipment, CategoryID still determines CategoryName. That remaining chain is the next step, not a reason to put CategoryName back in Reservation.

7. 3NF: remove the transitive dependency

Look inside Equipment. EquipmentID determines CategoryID, and CategoryID determines CategoryName. This extra step is the transitive dependency you now remove.

  1. Create Category with CategoryID as its key and CategoryName as its descriptive fact.
  2. Keep CategoryID in Equipment as a foreign key.
  3. Remove CategoryName from Equipment.

Borrower and Reservation already meet the intended 3NF conditions under the stated dependencies.

Borrower (BorrowerID, BorrowerLabel)

Category (CategoryID, CategoryName)

Equipment (EquipmentID, EquipmentDescription, CategoryID FK)

Reservation (BorrowerID FK, EquipmentID FK, ReservationDate, ReservationStatus)

CategoryIDCategoryName
C01Imaging
C02Support
C03Audio
EquipmentIDEquipmentDescriptionCategoryID
E01CameraC01
E02TripodC02
E03RecorderC03

The final four tables contain three borrower records, three category records, three equipment records and six reservation records. The requested equipment identifiers recur in Reservation because they represent relationships, not duplicated descriptive facts.

Under these exercise rules, each non-key fact depends on its table’s key without a dependency through another non-key fact. That is the reasoning for this design’s 3NF status; the number of tables alone proves nothing.

8. Verify that the split preserves information

Check that you can rebuild an original row. For B001/E01/1 May, follow the identifiers:

  1. Reservation gives you the status Confirmed.
  2. Borrower B001 gives you Learner A.
  3. Equipment E01 gives you Camera and category C01.
  4. Category C01 gives you Imaging.

You have recovered exactly the facts in the corresponding 1NF row.

Reconstruct all six rows. A correct decomposition preserves the intended records without missing rows or extra combinations. Keep the keys and references: joining on an ambiguous description such as Camera can create incorrect matches.

After decomposition, a new equipment item can be stored before it has reservations; updating a description changes one equipment record; deleting a reservation need not delete the equipment facts. Foreign-key constraints and deliberate deletion policies remain necessary.

9. Practice on a fresh four-table problem

A club register has MemberID, MemberLabel and a repeating list of activities: ActivityID, ActivityName, LeaderID, LeaderLabel, Term and AttendanceCount. A member can join the same activity once per term. An activity has one assigned leader under this exercise’s rules; a leader may lead several activities.

Dependencies: MemberID → MemberLabel; ActivityID → ActivityName, LeaderID; LeaderID → LeaderLabel; (MemberID, ActivityID, Term) → AttendanceCount. Write the 1NF relation, then 2NF and 3NF relations. Underline keys and mark FKs. Explain one partial and one transitive dependency.

Show the club model

1NF: flattened register with PK (MemberID, ActivityID, Term). 2NF: Member(MemberID PK, MemberLabel); Activity(ActivityID PK, ActivityName, LeaderID, LeaderLabel); Participation(MemberID PK/FK, ActivityID PK/FK, Term PK, AttendanceCount). 3NF: add Leader(LeaderID PK, LeaderLabel); retain LeaderID FK in Activity and remove LeaderLabel from Activity. MemberLabel depended only on MemberID; LeaderLabel depended transitively on ActivityID through LeaderID. Four tables remain.

10. Downloads and review checkpoints

Download student workbook Download explained answers

Download all stages: starter JSON and eight CSV tables · 1NF register only

At each stage, state the key, identify the dependency being removed and show where the moved fact now belongs. Keep the earlier model pack: these reservation tables are a learning extension, not a replacement for the existing loan datasets.

Course convention reference: SCSA support booklet, printed pages 17–21. Normalisation and data validation serve different purposes: a normalised database can still contain factually incorrect records.

11. Resolve update, insertion and deletion anomalies with evidence

Begin with business dependencies, not a rule that every repeated value is wrong. In the supplied flat membership table the key is (StudentID, ClubID). StudentID determines StudentName; ClubID determines ClubName and CoachID; CoachID determines CoachPhone. Each student may join many clubs, each club may have many students, and each club currently has one coach.

AnomalyFlat-table problemResolution and check
UpdateChanging T1's phone in only one membership leaves conflicting copiesUpdate one Coach row; all related clubs obtain that phone through a join
InsertionA new club with no members cannot be represented without inventing a student or breaking the membership keyInsert the Club independently, then add Membership rows when students join
DeletionDeleting the last Film membership loses Film's club/coach facts from the flat tableDelete the Membership only; Club and Coach records remain

The rows already have atomic values, so they can be in 1NF while still having anomalies. To reach 2NF for this composite-key design, separate Student and Club facts from Membership because they depend on only part of the key. At that stage Club may still store CoachPhone. To reach 3NF, separate Coach because ClubID determines CoachID which determines CoachPhone. The final relations are Student, Coach, Club and Membership. Keep linking keys and enforce relationships so decomposition does not disconnect facts.

Reconstruct the original memberships with a join before the independent insert/update/delete activities, checking both missing and extra rows. The fixture's repeated facts are consistent; real conflicting records require investigation. SELECT DISTINCT can suppress identical projections but cannot decide which conflicting phone number is true. A repeated foreign key is expected in a one-to-many relationship and is not by itself a normalisation error.

Pause and predict

If the final Film membership is deleted in the flat table, which facts disappear? Should deleting a membership mean the club no longer exists?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download anomalies_lab.sql

-- Fresh disposable SQLite database. Fixture dependencies are explicitly stated.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE FlatMembership (
    StudentID TEXT, StudentName TEXT, ClubID TEXT, ClubName TEXT,
    CoachID TEXT, CoachPhone TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
INSERT INTO FlatMembership VALUES
('S1', 'Ari', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S2', 'Bo', 'C1', 'Robotics', 'T1', '200'),
('S1', 'Ari', 'C2', 'Film', 'T2', '201');
CREATE TABLE Student (StudentID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, StudentName TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Coach (CoachID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, CoachPhone TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Club (
    ClubID TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ClubName TEXT NOT NULL,
    CoachID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Coach(CoachID)
);
CREATE TABLE Membership (
    StudentID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Student(StudentID),
    ClubID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Club(ClubID),
    PRIMARY KEY (StudentID, ClubID)
);
-- DISTINCT copies known-consistent fixture facts; it does not resolve conflicts.
INSERT INTO Student SELECT DISTINCT StudentID, StudentName FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Coach SELECT DISTINCT CoachID, CoachPhone FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Club SELECT DISTINCT ClubID, ClubName, CoachID FROM FlatMembership;
INSERT INTO Membership SELECT StudentID, ClubID FROM FlatMembership;
-- Capture a reconstruction before the independent modification activities.
CREATE TABLE ReconstructedBefore AS
SELECT s.StudentID, s.StudentName, c.ClubID, c.ClubName, t.CoachID, t.CoachPhone
FROM Membership AS m
JOIN Student AS s ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
JOIN Club AS c ON c.ClubID = m.ClubID
JOIN Coach AS t ON t.CoachID = c.CoachID;
UPDATE Coach SET CoachPhone = '299' WHERE CoachID = 'T1';
INSERT INTO Club VALUES ('C3', 'Coding', 'T1');
DELETE FROM Membership WHERE StudentID = 'S1' AND ClubID = 'C2';
SELECT ClubID, ClubName FROM Club ORDER BY ClubID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Draw arrows for each stated dependency. Complete the 1NF → 2NF → 3NF table splits, keeping keys visible. Predict a join that reconstructs each original membership exactly once.
  2. Independent transfer: Use the SQL fixture to add Coding with no members, update T1's phone once, and remove Film's last membership. Verify the club and coach survive. Transfer to Asset(AssetID, AssetName, RoomID, RoomName), where each RoomID determines one RoomName.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Given a new scenario, name the dependency causing each anomaly before proposing a split. Explain why atomic fields alone do not establish 3NF.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Club relation retains C1 Robotics, C2 Film and C3 Coding. C2 has no memberships but still exists. T1's phone becomes 299 in one Coach row. The asset transfer splits Room(RoomID PK, RoomName) and Asset(AssetID PK, AssetName, RoomID FK). Prove the relationships preserve the intended facts; do not delete repeated foreign keys.

12. Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence

Use the cases below as starting points, not a complete test plan. Write the expected outcome before running code, issuing SQL or revealing the explanation. For a conceptual claim, use the scenario and a counterexample; for implemented behaviour, record observed results. If the school has not run a check, label it pending.

Pause and predict

Choose one row and justify the expected outcome without using the program's output as your answer key.

Choose a case and predict first

  • Change a coach phone
  • Delete last club membership
Show expected evidence and why each case matters
Input / scenarioExpected evidenceWhy this case?
Change a coach phoneOne Coach update supplies joined reportsUpdate anomaly resolved
Delete last club membershipClub remains if the business rule retains itDeletion anomaly resolved

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete the first case with teacher modelling, the second with a partner, then swap explanations and challenge one assumption.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a third case that could expose an error the first two would miss. Record the expected and actual evidence, explain any mismatch, repair one cause and repeat both the new case and earlier cases.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The expected-evidence column gives the starting reference. A sound check explains the rule and its limits, not only a pass label. Keep a contrary or invalid case when appropriate, plus an unaffected case after a change. Your own actual-result evidence is still required.

Original ungraded teaching addition · 30 October 2026. Download examples and activity pack · Teacher guidance

Practice and explain

Identify

Why is BorrowerLabel a partial dependency in the 1NF register?

Show explained answer

It is determined by BorrowerID alone, which is only one part of the three-attribute reservation key.

Explain

Why is CategoryName still a problem in the 2NF Equipment table?

Show explained answer

EquipmentID determines CategoryID, and CategoryID determines CategoryName. That transitive dependency is removed by Category in 3NF.

Challenge

Is a table in 3NF just because it has four columns or a single ID key?

Show explained answer

No. Normal forms depend on keys and functional dependencies, not column count or the presence of an ID.

Distinguish

Should EquipmentID stop repeating in Reservation after 3NF?

Show explained answer

No. Repeated foreign-key values represent different reservation events. Remove inappropriate descriptive duplication, not legitimate history.

Test

Can normalisation prove that a recorded reservation date is true?

Show explained answer

No. It improves organisation and dependency structure. Validation and fact checking remain separate.

Your practical task

Complete the reservation transformation and the club transfer problem. For each stage, record keys, FKs, the dependency removed and an anomaly it reduces. Reconstruct two reservation rows through the final model and identify one rule that still needs enforcement.

Show illustrative answer / example

ReservationRegister becomes Borrower, Equipment and Reservation at 2NF. CategoryName moves from Equipment to Category at 3NF. Reservation’s PK is (BorrowerID, EquipmentID, ReservationDate), with BorrowerID/EquipmentID also FKs. Six original events remain. The club model ends with Member, Activity, Leader and Participation; Participation’s PK is (MemberID, ActivityID, Term). Availability/approval, valid dates and accurate facts still need checks beyond normalisation.

Check your understanding

Which change removes the transitive dependency in our 2NF Equipment table?

Delete all reservation history Give every field a different name Move CategoryName to Category and retain CategoryID as an Equipment FK

Quick-check answer and explanation

Move CategoryName to Category and retain CategoryID as an Equipment FK

CategoryID determines CategoryName. Give category facts their own keyed table while preserving the link from Equipment.

Chapter recap

Start with the business rules and a justified key. For 1NF, give each reservation one row with one value per field. For 2NF, remove partial dependencies. For 3NF, remove the remaining transitive dependency in this example. Rebuild the original rows to check that no facts were lost.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: retrieve keys; state reservation rules; identify repeating groups and anomalies; flatten to 1NF. Evidence: six atomic rows and a justified composite key.
  2. Lesson 2: read dependency statements; identify partial dependencies and form 2NF tables. Evidence: labelled keys/references and an explanation of each split.
  3. Lesson 3: remove CategoryName’s transitive dependency; reconstruct records from the four-table 3NF design. Evidence: reconstructed rows and anomaly explanations.
  4. Lesson 4: complete the club transfer problem independently, review explained answers and correct misconceptions. Evidence: stage-by-stage working. Four lessons total, with optional practice and explained answers.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 4 / CHAPTER 4

Getting started with SQL

Ask the equipment-loan database a question using SQL. You will choose columns, filter rows and sort the result, then compare it with the source records.

SQL / SQLITE CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Distinguish stored tables from query results.
  • Select fields and filter rows using comparisons and Boolean conditions.
  • Sort results with explicit direction and tie-break fields.
  • Check empty results, duplicates and boundary cases.

Before you start: Read related tables and recognise their identifiers.

Revisit if needed: Modelling entities and relationships.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

  2. Study the worked example: Make order and duplicates deliberate. Predict one step before reading its result.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Use the relational model

Suppose you want a list of camera items. You can ask the DBMS for that list using SQL, a language for querying data and changing database data or structure. In this chapter, you only read data.

Use the earlier loan model: Borrower has 4 rows, Category has 3, Equipment has 5 and Loan has 6. The reservation model from normalisation is a separate teaching example.

A query produces a result table. Selecting two fields does not delete other fields from the stored table. Python can submit SQL to a database, but SQL statements are not Python statements.

2. Open the starter database

Download SQLite starter Download complete SQL pack

  1. Save a working copy of sql-starter.sqlite.
  2. Open it in your school-approved SQLite-capable database application. This is a database file, not a CSV to import.
  3. Find its SQL editor, paste one query and run the selected statement.
  4. Compare the result columns, rows and order with this chapter.

Alternatively, create a new empty SQLite database and execute sql-setup.sql once. Re-running it in an existing database reports that tables already exist; use a new empty file to reset. For another DBMS, your teacher must adapt the setup and check its syntax.

SQLite-specific storage: DueDate is TEXT in fixed YYYY-MM-DD form; Returned is INTEGER, 0 for false and 1 for true, restricted by a CHECK. Dates are assumed valid in this supplied data; TEXT alone does not validate calendar dates. Enable foreign-key enforcement on each SQLite connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;. These are implementation choices, not universal SQL types.

3. Choose result columns with SELECT

Build your query in this order:

  1. Write SELECT and the field names you want, separated by commas.
  2. Write FROM and the table name.
  3. End the statement with a semicolon.

An asterisk requests every field. Naming fields makes the intended output clearer. SQL keywords are uppercase here to make them easier to spot.

SELECT * FROM Equipment ORDER BY EquipmentID;
EquipmentIDEquipmentDescriptionCategoryID
E01CameraC01
E02TripodC02
E03RecorderC03
E04CameraC01
E05MicrophoneC03
SELECT EquipmentID, EquipmentDescription FROM Equipment ORDER BY EquipmentID;
EquipmentIDEquipmentDescription
E01Camera
E02Tripod
E03Recorder
E04Camera
E05Microphone

The model contains two separate cameras, E01 and E04. Identical descriptions do not mean identical items.

4. Filter rows with WHERE

WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition. Use single quotes around text literals and = for equality. Do not quote a field name as a text value. Comparisons include <, <=, >, >= and <>.

SELECT EquipmentID, EquipmentDescription FROM Equipment WHERE EquipmentDescription = 'Camera' ORDER BY EquipmentID;
EquipmentIDEquipmentDescription
E01Camera
E04Camera

Predict before running: two matching rows, one per camera item. Filtering the result does not remove the other equipment records.

SELECT LoanID, DueDate FROM Loan WHERE Returned = 0 ORDER BY DueDate ASC, LoanID ASC;
LoanIDDueDate
L0012026-04-06
L0062026-04-07
L0022026-04-08
L0042026-04-10

In this file, Returned = 0 means still on loan. ASC sorts oldest due date first; LoanID breaks ties.

5. Combine conditions and test boundaries

For this exercise only, the reporting date is fixed at 8 April 2026. An overdue loan is unreturned and due before that date. A loan due on the reporting date is not yet overdue under this definition.

SELECT LoanID, BorrowerID, DueDate FROM Loan WHERE Returned = 0 AND DueDate < '2026-04-08' ORDER BY DueDate ASC, LoanID ASC;
LoanIDBorrowerIDDueDate
L001B0012026-04-06
L006B0042026-04-07

L002 is due on 8 April and is excluded by the strict < boundary. L005 has an earlier date but was returned. AND requires both conditions; OR allows either condition.

SELECT EquipmentID, CategoryID FROM Equipment WHERE CategoryID = 'C03' OR CategoryID = 'C01' ORDER BY EquipmentID;
EquipmentIDCategoryID
E01C01
E03C03
E04C01
E05C03
SELECT LoanID FROM Loan WHERE Returned = 0 AND (BorrowerID = 'B001' OR BorrowerID = 'B002') ORDER BY LoanID;
LoanID
L001
L002

Parentheses make the intended grouping clear. Without them, Returned = 0 AND BorrowerID = 'B001' OR BorrowerID = 'B002' also includes returned B002 loan L005 because AND binds more tightly than OR. Trace individual rows to check the logic.

Visual walkthrough

Trace an AND condition

Condition: Returned = 0 AND DueDate is before 8 April 2026.

Pause and predict: Which shown loans would an OR condition keep instead?

Show the explanation

All three. Each satisfies at least one condition: L002 is unreturned and L005 has an earlier due date.

Try a small change: Explain why OR would be the wrong condition for this overdue rule.

6. Make order and duplicates deliberate

If you need a predictable order, say so with ORDER BY, after WHERE. Use ASC for ascending order or DESC for descending order.

For example, two loans can have the same due date. Add a unique field such as LoanID to decide their order. Without ORDER BY, you must not rely on a particular row order.

DISTINCT removes duplicates from the selected result values, not the stored table. Two camera items still exist even when their shared description appears once.

SELECT DISTINCT EquipmentDescription FROM Equipment ORDER BY EquipmentDescription;
EquipmentDescription
Camera
Microphone
Recorder
Tripod

Selecting EquipmentID as well would keep all five items because the selected pairs differ. DISTINCT should not hide a modelling error.

7. Interpret empty results and debug

SELECT EquipmentID FROM Equipment WHERE CategoryID = 'C99' ORDER BY EquipmentID;

A valid query can return no records. Before changing its syntax, check whether any stored row should meet your condition. An empty result is different from an error such as a misspelt column name.

A valid query can return no records. Check the requirement and supplied values before assuming a syntax error. Compare this with an error such as a misspelt column or missing comma.

  1. Confirm the table and field names against the schema.
  2. Check commas, quotes and clause order.
  3. Run a simpler SELECT first, then add one condition at a time.
  4. Check row counts, boundary cases and tied sort values.

NULL is a missing/unknown value; test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, not = NULL. The required fields in this starter do not contain NULL. This distinction matters when later designs permit optional values.

8. Complete the independent query brief

The equipment desk wants a readable set of reports: all borrower identifiers/labels sorted by identifier; audio equipment IDs/descriptions; unreturned loan IDs/dates newest due date first, with LoanID breaking ties; and B002 loan IDs excluding returned records.

For each report, write the requirement in your own words, predict the result, run the query, record the actual result and explain any difference. Include a boundary explanation for the fixed-date overdue example.

Student workbook · Explained answers · Worked query file · Expected results

This introduces single-table queries. Database creation, inserts/updates/deletes, inner joins and aggregates continue in the database-solution chapter; this chapter alone does not cover the full database syllabus.

9. DDL and DML: change the structure, change the records

DDL changes database structure: CREATE TABLE defines a table, ALTER TABLE changes supported parts of its structure, and DROP TABLE removes a table. DML changes stored records: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows and DELETE removes matching rows. SELECT retrieves data; some classifications call it DQL, while others include retrieval within DML. State the operation's effect rather than relying only on a label.

OperationExample purposeEvidence to inspect
CREATE / ALTERAdd the Item schema and an Active fieldColumn definitions, defaults and rejected invalid data
INSERTAdd two identified itemsKeys, row count and relationship validity
UPDATE ... WHEREChange the cable price onlyTarget record and unchanged camera record
DELETE ... WHERERemove the disposable cable fixtureIts absence and other records' survival
ROLLBACKUndo a trial price changePreviously committed value restored
DROP TABLERemove the Scratch structureTable no longer exists; unlike DELETE, it does not retain an empty table

Run the download only in a fresh disposable SQLite database. Predict the affected rows before modifying data and SELECT the target plus a non-target afterwards. A WHERE clause can still be wrong: its presence alone is not proof of correctness. SQLite uses ALTER TABLE for supported structural changes; do not paste another DBMS's MODIFY syntax without checking its documentation. Transactions manage a related change; authorisation, validation and constraints remain separate responsibilities.

Pause and predict

After the trial camera price update is rolled back, is its price 0 or 40? Does DELETE remove the Item table?

SQLITE · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download ddl_dml_lab.sql

-- Run on a fresh disposable SQLite database, not a school production database.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE Supplier (
    SupplierID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    SupplierName TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE Item (
    ItemID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ItemName TEXT NOT NULL,
    Cost REAL NOT NULL CHECK (Cost >= 0),
    SupplierID INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Supplier(SupplierID)
);
ALTER TABLE Item ADD COLUMN Active INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (Active IN (0, 1));
INSERT INTO Supplier VALUES (1, 'North Supplies'), (2, 'West Supplies');
INSERT INTO Item (ItemID, ItemName, Cost, SupplierID)
VALUES (1, 'Camera', 40, 1), (2, 'Cable', 10, 1);
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 12 WHERE ItemID = 2;
DELETE FROM Item WHERE ItemID = 2 AND ItemName = 'Cable';
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE Item SET Cost = 0 WHERE ItemID = 1;
ROLLBACK;
CREATE TABLE Scratch (Note TEXT);
DROP TABLE Scratch;
SELECT ItemID, ItemName, Cost, Active FROM Item ORDER BY ItemID;

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Colour-code schema statements and record statements on paper. For each modification, identify target rows, expected state and one record/structure that should remain unchanged.
  2. Independent transfer: Use a fresh copy. Add an item, update only its cost, reject a negative cost using the constraint, and delete the disposable item. Inspect state after each operation. Compare DELETE FROM Scratch with DROP TABLE Scratch in separate fresh trials.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Without looking at the labels, explain what each SQL statement changes and design an unaffected-row test that would expose a missing or incorrect WHERE.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The final Item row is (1, Camera, 40, 1). The cable row was removed; rollback restores the camera price. Supplier still contains two rows. Scratch has been dropped. A negative cost is rejected by CHECK and must not alter the previously stored valid row. DELETE changes rows; DROP removes the structure.

Practice and explain

Explain

Does SELECT EquipmentID FROM Equipment remove other columns?

Show explained answer

No. It returns one column in the query result. Stored Equipment data remains unchanged.

Trace

Why is L005 excluded from the overdue report?

Show explained answer

Returned is 1. Its due date is early, but both parts of the AND condition must hold.

Boundary

Why is L002 excluded on 8 April 2026?

Show explained answer

Its due date equals the reporting date. The exercise defines overdue using a strict less-than comparison.

Distinguish

Why does DISTINCT EquipmentDescription return four rows rather than five?

Show explained answer

The five items have four different descriptions. Camera occurs twice in the stored table but once in that result.

Debug

Why use parentheses around the two borrower comparisons?

Show explained answer

They group the OR alternatives so Returned = 0 applies to both borrowers. Without grouping, the stated expression includes returned B002 records.

Your practical task

Complete the four equipment-desk reports in the workbook. Keep the SQL, predicted and actual results, and a short explanation of your filter and ordering for your own review. Explain one boundary test and one plausible query error.

Show illustrative answer / example

The borrower report returns B001–B004. Audio equipment is E03 Recorder and E05 Microphone. Active loans newest first are L004, L002, L006, L001. The active B002 report returns only L002. Use WHERE Returned = 0, not just an early date, for active/overdue logic. Exact queries and outputs are in the separate explained-answer download.

Check your understanding

Which condition matches an unreturned loan due before 8 April 2026?

Returned = 0 OR DueDate < '2026-04-08' Returned = 0 AND DueDate < '2026-04-08' Returned = 1 AND DueDate <= '2026-04-08'

Quick-check answer and explanation

Returned = 0 AND DueDate < '2026-04-08'

Both conditions must hold: unreturned and earlier than the fixed reporting date. OR also admits returned old loans or active loans that are not overdue.

Chapter recap

Build a query with SELECT and FROM, add WHERE when you need a filter, then use ORDER BY for a deliberate order. Predict the result before you run it. Check individual records, tied values and boundary dates. A SELECT result does not change the stored records.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 5–7 / CHAPTER 5

Building a database solution

Build a database that helps the equipment desk answer real questions. You will join related records, calculate summaries and make controlled changes, checking each result against a requirement.

SQL / PROJECT CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Create and explain a four-table relational implementation.
  • Use inner joins to produce readable loan reports.
  • Apply COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX to suitable records.
  • Use INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with checks and recovery.
  • Document and evaluate a database against acceptance criteria.

Before you start: Write SELECT queries and explain table keys and dependencies.

Revisit if needed: Getting started with SQL · Normalisation.

1. Define the equipment-desk solution

Start with what the desk needs to do:

  • Show active loans with readable borrower and item labels.
  • Report loan history by category.
  • Summarise inventory value and count each borrower’s loans.
  • Maintain records without losing valid history.

Turn each need into an acceptance criterion: a condition you can check to decide whether your solution works as intended.

The solution retains Borrower, Category, Equipment and Loan. Each loan records one item. LoanID identifies the event; BorrowerID and EquipmentID reference existing records. The project starter adds ReplacementCost to Equipment: fictional non-negative whole-dollar estimates of 600, 80, 150, 450 and 120 for E01–E05. These are teaching data, not current prices. No personal details are needed.

Weeks 5–6 teach and practice the required SQL. Week 7 launches the project; ten further build/testing lessons are embedded in weeks 8–12 while security teaching continues. Total project allocation: 14 lessons, including the four week-7 lessons.

2. Create and inspect four related tables

Download database project pack Download project starter

Open a working copy in a school-approved SQLite tool. To practice creation, execute database-project-setup.sql once in a new empty database. It creates four tables, loads the synthetic data and adds the cost field. Keep the SQL-basics database unchanged; this is a separate project edition.

CREATE TABLE Category (
  CategoryID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
  CategoryName TEXT NOT NULL
);

This statement creates a structure; INSERT adds records. Read the full setup file to identify each PK, FK, NOT NULL and CHECK. Create referenced tables before loading referencing rows. SQLite foreign-key enforcement must be enabled for each connection using PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, before starting a transaction.

DueDate remains valid YYYY-MM-DD TEXT in the supplied data, and Returned remains integer 0/1. The schema does not validate calendar dates or prevent overlapping loans. Document those limits and check them separately. A CHECK on cost rejects negative values, but does not make a positive estimate factually accurate.

3. Join keys to obtain readable reports

A join brings related rows together in a query result. It does not merge the stored tables. Start with one loan, read its borrower ID and find the borrower with that same ID. Repeat with the equipment ID.

The ON clause states which values must match. A name such as l.BorrowerID means “BorrowerID from the table labelled l”. These short labels are table aliases. An INNER JOIN keeps matching rows; a borrower without a loan has no row in this loan report.

SELECT l.LoanID, b.BorrowerLabel, e.EquipmentDescription, l.DueDate
FROM Loan AS l
INNER JOIN Borrower AS b ON l.BorrowerID = b.BorrowerID
INNER JOIN Equipment AS e ON l.EquipmentID = e.EquipmentID
WHERE l.Returned = 0
ORDER BY l.DueDate, l.LoanID;
LoanIDBorrowerLabelEquipmentDescriptionDueDate
L001Learner ACamera2026-04-06
L006Learner DMicrophone2026-04-07
L002Learner BTripod2026-04-08
L004Learner CCamera2026-04-10

L001 joins to B001 and E01. There are four active loan rows, not four distinct borrowers or item descriptions. A borrower may appear more than once. Omitting a join condition can combine unrelated rows; matching descriptions instead of identifiers is unreliable.

SELECT l.LoanID, e.EquipmentID, c.CategoryName
FROM Loan AS l
INNER JOIN Equipment AS e ON l.EquipmentID = e.EquipmentID
INNER JOIN Category AS c ON e.CategoryID = c.CategoryID
ORDER BY l.LoanID;
LoanIDEquipmentIDCategoryName
L001E01Imaging
L002E02Support
L003E03Audio
L004E04Imaging
L005E02Support
L006E05Audio

E02 occurs in two loan events, L002 and L005. Both belong in history. One equipment record can match several loans; this is expected rather than a duplicate item to delete.

Worked walkthrough

Follow one loan through its keys

Use the stored identifiers rather than matching display names.

Pause and predict: L002 and L005 both refer to E02. Should a loan-history report keep both?

Show the explanation

Yes. They are different loan events. Repeating an equipment ID across events is expected.

Try a small change: Trace L003 through its borrower, item and category before running the query.

4. Summarise the right records

Before you calculate a total, ask what one input row represents. For inventory value, you need one row per equipment item, so calculate from Equipment.

If you join equipment to loan history first, E02 appears in two loan events. Adding both rows would count the same item twice. This is a row-level mistake even when the SQL runs successfully.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ItemCount, SUM(ReplacementCost) AS TotalCost,
       AVG(ReplacementCost) AS MeanCost, MIN(ReplacementCost) AS LowestCost,
       MAX(ReplacementCost) AS HighestCost
FROM Equipment;
ItemCountTotalCostMeanCostLowestCostHighestCost
51400280.080600

These five costs total 1400; the mean is 280, with minimum 80 and maximum 600. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(field) counts non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULL values. Keep numeric data numeric; averaging IDs has no useful interpretation.

SELECT b.BorrowerID, b.BorrowerLabel, COUNT(*) AS LoanCount
FROM Borrower AS b
INNER JOIN Loan AS l ON b.BorrowerID = l.BorrowerID
GROUP BY b.BorrowerID, b.BorrowerLabel
ORDER BY b.BorrowerID;
BorrowerIDBorrowerLabelLoanCount
B001Learner A2
B002Learner B2
B003Learner C1
B004Learner D1

GROUP BY makes a separate summary for each borrower represented in loan history. List both displayed non-aggregate borrower fields in GROUP BY. It is an extension to support the report, not a reason to select arbitrary ungrouped fields.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS ItemCount, SUM(ReplacementCost) AS TotalCost,
       AVG(ReplacementCost) AS MeanCost, MIN(ReplacementCost) AS LowestCost,
       MAX(ReplacementCost) AS HighestCost
FROM Equipment WHERE CategoryID = 'C99';
ItemCountTotalCostMeanCostLowestCostHighestCost
0NULLNULLNULLNULL

An ungrouped aggregate still produces one summary row for empty input: COUNT is 0 and these other aggregates are NULL. NULL is not automatically zero. A GROUP BY query with no input groups returns no rows.

Visual walkthrough

One item can appear in several loan events

E02 has an estimated replacement cost of 80 whole dollars.

Pause and predict: Why does the full joined loan-history total equal 1480 rather than the inventory total of 1400?

Show the explanation

E02 appears in two loan events, so its 80 is included twice. The other items appear once in this supplied history.

Try a small change: Suppose E01 gets another loan event. Explain how the joined-history total changes while the inventory total stays the same.

5. Insert a new record deliberately

INSERT supplies a value for each named field. B005 is a fictional new borrower, absent from the original starter. Execute this exercise on a working copy; do not run the same insert twice expecting another borrower.

INSERT INTO Borrower (BorrowerID, BorrowerLabel) VALUES ('B005', 'Learner E');

After insertion, selecting B005 shows one row and there are five borrowers. Reusing B005 fails the primary-key constraint. Adding a Loan with B999 fails the foreign-key constraint when enforcement is enabled. Existing item/borrower references must be valid before a new loan is inserted.

6. Update the intended row and check it

The desk has confirmed that L001’s item was returned. Its current Returned value is 0. Make the change in three steps:

  1. Use SELECT to inspect L001 before changing it.
  2. Use the same key condition in UPDATE to set Returned to 1.
  3. Check L001 again and confirm that other loan rows are unchanged.
SELECT LoanID, Returned FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 'L001';
UPDATE Loan SET Returned = 1 WHERE LoanID = 'L001';
SELECT LoanID, Returned FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 'L001';

Expected before/after: L001 changes from 0 to 1. Other loan rows stay unchanged; active loan count falls from four to three. An UPDATE without WHERE affects every row. A valid statement can match zero rows, so inspect the result rather than assuming success.

7. Delete only the disposable test record

In this rehearsal, B005 is a disposable borrower with no loans. Confirm the target, delete it and check it is gone.

SELECT * FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';
DELETE FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';
SELECT * FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';

The final query returns no rows. DELETE without WHERE removes every row allowed by the constraints. Deleting referenced B001 is rejected by this starter’s foreign-key policy; do not disable enforcement to make it succeed. Deleting a returned loan would erase history, so the desk’s routine return operation updates Returned instead.

8. Rehearse and recover with a transaction

Open a fresh project copy with no active transaction. Run the provided rehearsal a statement at a time so you can inspect changes. BEGIN starts the group; ROLLBACK undoes its changes. The supplied script ends with ROLLBACK to restore the starting records.

-- Run in a working project copy, outside an existing transaction.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO Borrower (BorrowerID, BorrowerLabel) VALUES ('B005', 'Learner E');
SELECT * FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';
SELECT LoanID, Returned FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 'L001';
UPDATE Loan SET Returned = 1 WHERE LoanID = 'L001';
SELECT LoanID, Returned FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 'L001';
DELETE FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';
SELECT COUNT(*) AS RemainingTestBorrowers FROM Borrower WHERE BorrowerID = 'B005';
ROLLBACK;
-- Original four borrowers and L001 Returned = 0 are restored.

Use COMMIT to keep the changes only after your checks pass. If a statement fails during practice, stop and inspect the transaction state. Use ROLLBACK if the practice transaction is still active.

Do not assume one failed statement undoes earlier successful statements. Some tools manage transactions for you, so check how your tool behaves.

A transaction is not a backup of earlier committed work. Keep a known-good closed database copy and test restoring it. Do not copy a database file casually while another connection is writing.

9. Test against requirements, then transfer

For each requirement, decide how you will check it before running the test. Record the requirement, input or action, expected outcome, actual evidence and pass/fail result in a test log.

Include ordinary cases, boundaries, invalid references, duplicate IDs, negative costs, an empty report and recovery. Use fresh copies or roll back between tests so an earlier change cannot silently alter the next test’s starting state.

Independent report: list active loans with LoanID, BorrowerLabel, EquipmentID, CategoryName and DueDate, oldest first; then show inventory totals for each category. Explain why the inventory summary must not count loan events.

Transfer: add an unused synthetic borrower in a transaction. Predict whether the inner-join borrower count report will display them, check the prediction, then roll back. It will omit them because no Loan row matches. Reporting every borrower including zero-loan borrowers would require a different query design.

10. Launch, document and evaluate the project

Student project brief · Practice workbook · Explained answers and teacher checkpoints · Test-log template

For your self-review, bring together your four-table database, creation/data SQL, ER diagram and data dictionary, saved report queries, before/after evidence for modifications, tests and evaluation against your acceptance criteria. A GUI or Python interface is optional; the core task is the database.

Week 7: confirm requirements, review the design, create/load the database and demonstrate the first report. Weeks 8–10: use two workshops each week to build reports, practice controlled changes and apply taught security controls. Weeks 11–12: use two each week to test, recover, document and evaluate. No extra major project or compulsory homework is assumed.

The starter schema is a worked scaffold. To practice database creation, run and explain your own creation script and justify any adaptations. A supplied file can help you start, but it cannot explain your choices for you. Privacy/security design decisions are revisited after explicit security lessons. This is an optional learning project with explained checkpoints; teacher review remains pending.
