11. Bridge Python to a controlled SQL change

Use the example as a worked model, then fade the support: predict on paper, trace one execution together, change one requirement and test independently. The code is ordinary Python 3 and runs offline. Work in a disposable learning folder. These are ungraded practice examples, not additional assessment requirements.

Record the input or initial state, expected outcome, actual outcome, pass/fail and a reason. Where an invalid input is outside the function's stated contract, explain that precondition rather than silently inventing behaviour.

Pause and predict

Will the apostrophe be part of the stored name or break the statement?

PYTHON 3 · WORKED EXAMPLE

Download parameterised_database.py

import sqlite3
with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    connection.execute("CREATE TABLE Member (MemberID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name TEXT NOT NULL)")
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO Member VALUES (?, ?)", (1, "O'Neil"))
    connection.execute("UPDATE Member SET Name = ? WHERE MemberID = ?", ("O'Neill", 1))
    rows = connection.execute("SELECT Name FROM Member WHERE MemberID = ?", (1,)).fetchall()
    print(rows)
    assert connection.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Member").fetchone()[0] == 1
print("targeted update checked")
Show expected output after your prediction
[("O'Neill",)]
targeted update checked

14. Create a fresh relational database independently

Running a supplied creation script demonstrates setup, not independent schema construction. Use a fresh context after the worked equipment database: Author has many Titles, and each Title has exactly one Author. Define a required foreign key with compatible types and test enforcement on the actual connection. The independent task below adds a different many-to-many design rather than merely renaming this example.

Worked example

-- Worked example: run only in a new disposable SQLite database
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE Author(AuthorID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, Name TEXT NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE Title(TitleID TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL, AuthorID TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES Author(AuthorID), Name TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO Author VALUES('A1','Mia');
INSERT INTO Title VALUES('T1','A1','Robots');
SELECT t.TitleID,a.Name FROM Title t INNER JOIN Author a ON t.AuthorID=a.AuthorID;
-- Expected: T1 | Mia

Insert M1/Ari, W1/Robotics and their enrolment. Write a joined report and demonstrate duplicate-pair and missing-M9 rejection with foreign keys enabled before the transaction.

Show explained answer

Use three CREATE TABLE statements; text keys explicitly NOT NULL; Enrolment PRIMARY KEY(MemberID,WorkshopID) plus two NOT NULL REFERENCES constraints. Insert parent rows before child. Practice and explain

Trace

Why can E02 appear twice in the history report?

Show explained answer

L002 and L005 are different loan events linked to the same equipment item. A one-to-many match is expected.

Explain

Why calculate inventory value directly from Equipment?

Show explained answer

Each equipment item occurs once there. Joining to loan history can repeat items and distort totals.

Predict

What happens to the borrower report when B005 has no loans?

Show explained answer

The inner-join report omits B005 because it has no matching Loan row.

Distinguish

What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(field)?

Show explained answer

COUNT(*) counts result rows; COUNT(field) excludes rows where that field is NULL.

Recover

Does a failed statement guarantee that earlier changes have been undone?

Show explained answer

No. Stop, inspect the transaction state and roll back an active practice transaction. The rehearsal explicitly ends with ROLLBACK.

Your practical task

Complete the workbook, then launch the project using the brief. Demonstrate a joined report, an inventory summary, checked modifications and recovery. Supply ER/data dictionary documentation and a test log with actual evidence.

Show illustrative answer / example

The original active report has four rows. Inventory summary is five items, total 1400, mean 280, minimum 80 and maximum 600. Updating L001 to Returned = 1 leaves three active loans. The B005 insert/delete rehearsal ends with rollback, restoring four borrowers and L001 Returned = 0. Keep report evidence and project changes separate from the untouched starter.

Check your understanding

Where should the total replacement cost of the five inventory items be calculated?

From Equipment, with one row per item From Loan history, summing every joined event From borrower labels using AVG

Quick-check answer and explanation

From Equipment, with one row per item

Inventory value concerns equipment items. Loan history can repeat an item, so summing after that join can count it more than once.

Chapter recap

Start with a requirement you can check. Join records using the intended identifiers and calculate summaries from the right rows. Preview a change, make it, then check the result. Use transactions for controlled practice and test a restored backup for recovery.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Week 5, lesson 1: trace key matches; build the active-loan inner join.
  2. Week 5, lesson 2: join categories; diagnose missing/wrong matches.
  3. Week 5, lesson 3: aggregate inventory; distinguish row counts and numeric summaries.
  4. Week 5, lesson 4: independent joined/category reports and feedback.
  5. Week 6, lesson 1: inspect creation SQL; run it in a new database; test keys/checks.
  6. Week 6, lesson 2: INSERT and UPDATE with before/after evidence.
  7. Week 6, lesson 3: DELETE disposable records; transaction/recovery rehearsal.
  8. Week 6, lesson 4: controlled SQL practice; explain and repair errors.
  9. Week 7, lesson 1: project requirements and acceptance criteria.
  10. Week 7, lesson 2: ER diagram/data dictionary and design checkpoint.
  11. Week 7, lesson 3: create/load a working database and first reports.
  12. Week 7, lesson 4: demonstrate the initial build and plan the ten later workshops.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 8–11 / CHAPTER 6

Threats and protective measures

Work out what happened before choosing a security control. You will use the equipment desk to explain threats, access controls and encryption, then practice historical ciphers to see their limits.

CYBER SECURITY CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Use CIA to explain security impacts and AAA to audit access.
  • Distinguish the named network threats and malware types.
  • Justify layered controls, authentication and encryption choices.
  • Use rotation, random substitution and Vigenère ciphers with stated conventions.
  • Record evidence and limitations in the database project.

Before you start: Recognise the equipment-desk records and use a separate database copy for recovery practice.

Revisit if needed: Relational database foundations · Building a database solution.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Begin with assets, threats and evidence

Imagine the desk cannot open its database. You know the service is unavailable, but you do not yet know why. A power failure, accidental deletion or malicious attack could be involved.

Use these terms to organise your explanation:

  • Asset: something valuable, such as accurate loan records.
  • Threat: something that can cause harm.
  • Vulnerability: a weakness that could allow harm.
  • Risk: the likelihood of harm and its consequence.
  • Incident: an event affecting security.

State what is known, what is inferred and what is still uncertain. Accidental deletion and a power failure can affect security goals even without a malicious attacker.

2. Analyse harm using the CIA triad

CIA groups three security goals: confidentiality, integrity and availability. Ask what happened to the information or service, rather than choosing a label from the incident name alone.

GoalMeaningDesk example
ConfidentialityInformation is accessible only to those authorised to see it.A loan export is disclosed to an unauthorised person.
IntegrityInformation and systems are protected against unauthorised alteration or destruction.A loan is falsely marked returned.
AvailabilityAuthorised users can access the needed service/data when required.The desk cannot open the database.

One event can affect several goals. Ransomware can disrupt availability; stolen data can also affect confidentiality. Explain the particular consequence rather than assigning exactly one letter to every threat. Accurate-looking data is not proof that access was authorised.

3. Audit access using AAA

PartQuestionEvidence/control
AuthenticationWho or what is requesting access?Individual sign-in and appropriate factors.
AuthorisationWhat is that identity permitted to do?Clerk may maintain loans; reviewer may read reports.
AccountingWhat activity is recorded for accountability?Identity, action, target, outcome and time in protected logs.

AAA accounting is activity tracking, not financial bookkeeping. Successful authentication does not grant unlimited permission. Shared accounts weaken attribution. Logs support investigation but need access controls, reliable time and review; avoid recording passwords or unnecessary personal data.

The classroom SQLite file does not automatically provide per-user roles, application login or an audit trail. File permissions and the surrounding application/service matter. Describe a control as implemented only when there is evidence.

4. Distinguish people, network and application threats

ThreatDistinguishing mechanismScenarioProtective measure and limit
Social engineering / phishingManipulates a person into revealing information or taking an unsafe action; phishing uses deceptive messages or sites.Fake equipment-desk sign-in request.Independent verification, reporting practice and MFA; training alone does not eliminate deception.
Denial of serviceExhausts or disrupts resources so legitimate users cannot use a service; distributed DoS involves multiple sources.Loan portal overwhelmed by requests.Traffic filtering/rate limits and provider support; ordinary backups do not keep the live service reachable.
Back doorA concealed or unintended route that bypasses normal access controls.Undocumented maintenance account bypasses normal login.Remove unnecessary access paths, review accounts/configuration and monitor use.
IP spoofingFalsifies a packet’s source IP address; this does not prove the sender can receive replies or has authenticated.Traffic claims to come from a trusted address.Use authenticated communication and appropriate ingress/egress filtering; do not treat an IP address alone as identity.
SQL injectionUntrusted input is treated as SQL structure by an application.A search form builds a query by concatenating input.Parameterised statements and least database privilege; field validation is an additional check.
Man-in-the-middleAn intermediary intercepts and may alter communication between parties.A false network intermediary relays portal traffic.Authenticated encrypted connections, verified endpoints and certificate checks.
Cross-site scripting (XSS)Untrusted content becomes executable script in a user’s browser through a vulnerable application.A portal displays submitted notes as active page content.Context-appropriate output encoding, safe DOM/template practices and sanitisation where HTML is allowed. SQL parameters do not prevent browser script execution.

Mechanism distinguishes SQL injection from XSS: one changes database commands; the other executes content in a browser. IP spoofing is about an address claim; it is not equivalent to logging in. A back door can enable access without the normal route.

5. Distinguish malware, physical threats and new flaws

TypeDistinguishing featureScenarioProtective measure and limit
VirusMalicious code attaches to a host such as a file/program and spreads when the host executes.Infected program copied between desk devices.Trusted software, updates and endpoint protection.
WormMalware that can propagate between systems without attaching to a host file.Malware spreads between vulnerable devices.Patching, segmentation and endpoint protection.
Trojan horseMalicious software disguised as a useful or legitimate program; the label describes deception, not self-replication.Fake inventory utility installs unwanted code.Approved software sources, application controls and limited privilege.
SpywareCovertly collects information or monitors activity.Software records desk activity or credentials.Endpoint protection, permissions review and trusted software.
AdwareSoftware that displays advertising; unwanted or malicious variants can track users or disrupt work.Unwanted advertising bundled with a utility.Review installations, permissions and trusted sources; not every advertising-supported application is malware.
RansomwareMalware that blocks access, often by encrypting data, and demands payment; attacks may also steal data.Loan database becomes unreadable and an extortion message appears.Prevention controls plus protected, tested backups and an incident plan; restoring data does not undo a disclosure.
Physical security threatPhysical access, theft, damage or environmental disruption can compromise a system.Unlocked desk laptop is stolen; a power loss interrupts service.Restricted access, locked storage, screen locks, suitable power protection and recovery arrangements.
Zero-day vulnerabilityA previously unknown vulnerability may be exploited before defenders have a practical fix. It is a weakness, not a malware category.A newly disclosed application flaw has no patch available yet.Reduce exposure, use temporary mitigations and monitoring, then apply a verified fix when available.

Labels can overlap: a Trojan may install spyware or ransomware. Virus and worm describe spread; ransomware describes a harmful outcome. Zero-day describes vulnerability timing. Identify the feature stated in the scenario and justify it.

6. Choose layers of protection

Choose a control that addresses how the harm could happen. A backup can help after data loss, but it cannot stop someone being deceived by a phishing message.

  • Preventive controls reduce the chance of harm.
  • Detective controls help you notice an event.
  • Corrective and recovery controls help restore safe operation afterwards.

Using several suitable controls creates layers of protection.

ControlUseful purposeRemaining limit
Updates and trusted softwareReduce known flaws and unwanted code.No guarantee against an unknown vulnerability.
Least privilege and separate rolesLimit permitted actions and potential damage.An authorised user can still make a mistake.
Monitoring and protected logsDetect unusual activity and support investigation.Logs need review; alerts can be incomplete.
Protected backups and restore testsRecover usable data after loss.Recent changes may be lost; disclosure remains.
Physical controls and device protectionReduce theft and unauthorised physical access.Signed-in/unlocked devices may expose usable data.
Authenticated encrypted communicationReduce interception/alteration in transit.A compromised endpoint or deceived user is still a risk.

For the project, prioritise controls using the asset and plausible impact. State cost, usability and residual risk. Do not promise that a firewall, encryption or antivirus prevents every threat.

Worked walkthrough

Match the control to how harm happens

A control is useful when you can explain the link between the weakness, its action and the remaining risk.

Pause and predict: Would adding MFA alone remove a role’s excessive export rights?

Show the explanation

No. MFA strengthens authentication. The allowed export operation must also be restricted through authorisation.

Try a small change: Choose one scenario and write a test for required access plus a test for access that should be refused.

7. Protect authentication and set a useful policy

Use long, unique passwords/passphrases; avoid predictable personal details and reuse. A password manager can help manage unique credentials. An organisational policy should address enrolment, minimum requirements, MFA, account recovery, suspected compromise and account removal, rather than relying only on a complexity slogan.

Check the types of evidence a sign-in uses. A password and a PIN are both something you know, so combining them is not two-factor authentication.

Two-factor authentication combines two different categories: something you know, something you have, or something you are. A password plus an appropriately bound device authenticator can combine knowledge and possession.

MFA reduces risk, but deception or weak account recovery can still defeat protection.

Biometrics use characteristics such as a fingerprint. Consider false acceptance/rejection, accessibility and protection of biometric templates; biological traits are hard to replace after exposure. Do not collect classmates’ passwords or biometric samples for this activity. Modern policy choices should be justified using current guidance rather than assuming frequent forced password changes solve every problem.

Reference: ASD passphrase guidance.

Visual walkthrough

Count factor categories, not secrets

Two-factor authentication uses evidence from two different categories.

Pause and predict: Does a password plus a second password provide two-factor authentication?

Show the explanation

No. Both are knowledge factors. You need evidence from two distinct categories.

Try a small change: Describe a knowledge-plus-possession combination, then explain one remaining risk.

8. Explain encryption and key roles

If you want only the intended recipient to read a message, you can encrypt it. Encryption transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key. Decryption uses the appropriate key to recover the plaintext. These are techniques within cryptography.

Do not confuse encryption with encoding a file format. Cryptographic hashing is different too: it produces a digest and is designed to make finding an input from a given digest computationally infeasible. It is not reversible encryption.

ApproachKey relationshipExample reasoning
Symmetric encryptionThe same secret key is used to encrypt and decrypt.Suitable for bulk data, but the shared secret must be protected/distributed securely.
Asymmetric/public-key encryptionA related public/private key pair has different roles.For confidentiality to a recipient, encrypt with their verified public key; the recipient decrypts with their private key.

Keep private keys private; verify who a public key belongs to. Digital signatures use different operations to support authenticity/integrity and do not simply mean keeping the message secret. Real protocols can combine asymmetric key establishment/authentication with symmetric data encryption.

Encryption at rest and in transit protect different situations. Encryption does not automatically provide authorisation, safe input handling, backups or every form of integrity protection. Historical ciphers below are learning tools, not protection for the project database.

9. Use a rotation cipher with explicit conventions

To encrypt with a rotation cipher, move every letter forward by the same number of places. That number is the key, k. This is a substitution cipher with a fixed rotation.

  1. Use uppercase A–Z and remove spaces and punctuation.
  2. Convert letters to numbers: A = 0 through Z = 25.
  3. Add k and wrap around modulo 26.
  4. Convert the result back to a letter. To decrypt, subtract k instead.
Plaintext:  LOAN
Key shift:  3
Ciphertext: ORDQ
Trace: L(11)+3=O(14); O(14)+3=R(17);
       A(0)+3=D(3); N(13)+3=Q(16)

Wrap-around: Z with shift 3 becomes C. Decrypt ORDQ using shift 3 to recover LOAN. With 26 letters there are only 26 possible shifts including 0, so trying each is feasible. A short result may need context to identify the intended plaintext.

10. Use a random substitution and compare patterns

A monoalphabetic random substitution uses one shuffled alphabet as a one-to-one mapping. The mapping below is fixed for this exercise; each plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter.

Plain:  ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
Cipher: QWERTYUIOPASDFGHJKLZXCVBNM
LOAN → SGQF

Decrypt by reversing the mapping, not by applying it again. It has far more possible keys than a rotation cipher, but repeated letters and language patterns remain. Frequency analysis compares observed letter/pattern frequencies with plausible language patterns; the most common ciphertext symbol is not guaranteed to mean E, especially in short messages.

11. Use a polyalphabetic cipher

In a Vigenère exercise, repeat a keyword to supply a different shift at each position. Use A = 0, the same uppercase letters-only convention, and a forward shift for encryption.

Plaintext:  LOAN
Repeated key: KEYK
Shifts:       10 4 24 10
Ciphertext:  VSYX

Subtract each corresponding key shift to decrypt. A plaintext letter can encrypt differently at different positions. This weakens simple single-alphabet frequency analysis, but a repeated key creates patterns that can be analysed; historical Vigenère is not modern secure encryption.

Practice: rotate RETURN by 5; apply the supplied substitution to LOAN; encrypt DATA with key KEY (repeat as KEYK). Explain brute force versus frequency analysis using these conventions.

12. Work through an incident using evidence

The desk finds an unapproved return-status change. Everyone shares a login and no application audit trail exists. Known: the value changed and attribution is weak. Unknown: who changed it, whether it was intentional and whether any data was disclosed.

CIA: integrity is affected. AAA: shared authentication and missing accounting make attribution weak; review whether authorisation allowed too many people to edit. Proposed controls: individual accounts, limited modification roles, protected change records and periodic reconciliation.

Verify against a known record, preserve relevant evidence and follow the school’s reporting process. An affected system may need controlled isolation by authorised staff. Record the justified response and limitations; do not accuse someone from an IP address or timestamp alone.

13. Apply the controls to the database project

In the two project workshops each week, turn the security reasoning into evidence: identify assets/roles, list allowed actions, protect a known-good backup and test restoration in a separate copy. Mark controls as implemented, tested or proposed.

For a file-based SQLite project, explain who can read/copy/modify the file under the actual environment. A decorative login screen does not stop someone opening an accessible database file directly. If extending with Python, pass values through query parameters; do not concatenate input into SQL structure.

cursor.execute(
    "SELECT LoanID FROM Loan WHERE BorrowerID = ?",
    (borrower_id,)
)

This SQLite Python example binds one value. It does not parameterise table names or implement authorisation. For a web extension, render untrusted text safely for its output context; parameterised SQL does not stop XSS.

14. Practice on the scenario pack

Download student workbook Download explained answers

Eight incident scenarios · Risk/control template · Cipher exercises · Complete security pack

For each scenario: name the mechanism, cite the evidence, explain CIA impact, apply AAA where relevant, propose a matching control and state a limitation. Keep uncertainty visible. These are synthetic desk exercises using paper or local sample files; no live-system attacks are required.

Weeks 8–11 use two explicit security lessons and two project workshops per week. Week 12 continues with responsible data use, privacy and ethical hacking; this chapter does not establish full Unit 2 coverage.

Source checks: 2026 SCSA Year 11 syllabus, OWASP SQL injection prevention, OWASP XSS prevention and NIST terminology.

15. Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence

Use the cases below as starting points, not a complete test plan. Write the expected outcome before running code, issuing SQL or revealing the explanation. For a conceptual claim, use the scenario and a counterexample; for implemented behaviour, record observed results. If the school has not run a check, label it pending.

Pause and predict

Choose one row and justify the expected outcome without using the program's output as your answer key.

Choose a case and predict first

  • Unexpected executable attachment
  • Restore into an infected environment
Show expected evidence and why each case matters
Input / scenarioExpected evidenceWhy this case?
Unexpected executable attachmentDo not run; follow reporting processPreventive behaviour
Restore into an infected environmentContain/clean first; verify clean recoveryBackup is not prevention

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete the first case with teacher modelling, the second with a partner, then swap explanations and challenge one assumption.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a third case that could expose an error the first two would miss. Record the expected and actual evidence, explain any mismatch, repair one cause and repeat both the new case and earlier cases.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.
Show the explanation and checking guidance

The expected-evidence column gives the starting reference. A sound check explains the rule and its limits, not only a pass label. Keep a contrary or invalid case when appropriate, plus an unaffected case after a change. Your own actual-result evidence is still required.

Original ungraded teaching addition · 30 October 2026. Download examples and activity pack · Teacher guidance

Practice and explain

Distinguish

Is a password plus a PIN necessarily two-factor authentication?

Show explained answer

No. Both are knowledge factors. Two-factor authentication needs two distinct categories.

Analyse

Does ransomware necessarily prove that information was stolen?

Show explained answer

No. Availability may be affected by encryption. Confidentiality requires evidence of access/disclosure; some ransomware attacks also steal data.

Explain

Why does parameterised SQL not prevent every XSS flaw?

Show explained answer

SQL parameters keep values separate from database commands. XSS concerns unsafe execution of content in a browser and requires suitable output handling.

Audit

Does a successful login prove the user may delete loan history?

Show explained answer

No. Authentication checks identity; authorisation determines permitted actions. Accounting records activity.

Compare

Why is the shuffled substitution alphabet still vulnerable?

Show explained answer

One mapping preserves repeated-letter and language patterns. Frequency analysis can exploit them; short texts can remain ambiguous.

Your practical task

Analyse four unfamiliar scenarios and complete the cipher exercises. For the database project, produce an asset/role/control register and demonstrate a restore using a separate sample copy. Label implemented, tested and proposed controls, with evidence and residual risk.

Show illustrative answer / example

A justified response connects mechanism → asset and CIA impact → relevant AAA weakness → matching control → limitation. Shared credentials weaken attribution; a clean backup supports recovery but cannot undo disclosure. Cipher checks: LOAN/shift 3 gives ORDQ; RETURN/shift 5 gives WJYZWS; supplied substitution LOAN gives SGQF; DATA/key KEY gives NERK.

Check your understanding

An authorised account reads reports but is blocked from changing loans. Which AAA component determines that restriction?

Authentication Authorisation Accounting

Quick-check answer and explanation

Authorisation

Authorisation defines permitted actions. Authentication checks identity and accounting records activity.

Chapter recap

State what you know about an event, then explain its mechanism and possible impact. CIA describes security goals; AAA separates identity checks, permissions and activity records. Match controls to the risk and explain their limits. Historical ciphers help you study patterns, but they cannot protect real database records.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Week 8, lesson 1: asset/threat/vulnerability/risk; CIA incident analysis.
  2. Week 8, lesson 2: AAA audit of shared accounts; define roles and evidence. Lessons 3–4 are project workshops.
  3. Week 9, lesson 1: compare people/network/application threats using mechanism cards.
  4. Week 9, lesson 2: malware/physical/zero-day scenarios; justify controls and limits. Lessons 3–4 are project workshops.
  5. Week 10, lesson 1: password policy, two-factor categories and biometric trade-offs.
  6. Week 10, lesson 2: symmetric/asymmetric encryption and key roles. Lessons 3–4 are project workshops.
  7. Week 11, lesson 1: trace rotation and random-substitution ciphers; brute force and frequency reasoning.
  8. Week 11, lesson 2: Vigenère transfer and explained corrections. Lessons 3–4 are project testing/recovery workshops.

UNIT 2 / WEEK 12 / CHAPTER 7

Responsible data use

Decide what the equipment desk should collect, who may use it and what may be shared. You will connect privacy, security and ethical testing to practical choices, using evidence to explain each decision.

PRIVACY / ETHICS CLASSROOM DRAFT · REVIEW PENDING

What you’ll learn

  • Distinguish privacy, security, ethical and legal decisions.
  • Recognise personal/sensitive information and re-identification risks.
  • Apply selected APPs as a course lens while identifying jurisdiction limits.
  • Explain authorisation and scope in ethical hacking/penetration testing.
  • Evaluate project criteria using actual evidence and stated limitations.

Before you start: Explain confidentiality, integrity, availability and access permissions.

Revisit if needed: Threats and protective measures.

Required skills, support-booklet material and enrichment · Find reviewed teaching and practice.

Find this chapter’s activities and downloads.

Revise this topic: checklist and closed-book retrieval.

1. Separate privacy, security, ethics and law

A loan register can be securely stored yet still collect information it does not need. To explain a decision, ask four different questions:

  • Privacy: how is information about people collected, used, disclosed and controlled?
  • Security: how are the information and systems protected?
  • Ethics: is the decision fair, justified and responsible?
  • Law: which obligations apply in this situation?

For the equipment desk, start with purpose: record and manage item loans. Ask which people are affected, what information is needed, who will see it and how someone can challenge an error. A technically valid record or successful query does not settle those questions.

2. Recognise personal and sensitive information

Look beyond names when deciding whether a record identifies someone. A borrower ID linked to a school roster, exact dates or a distinctive borrowing pattern may identify a person.

Personal information is information about an identified person or someone reasonably identifiable in the circumstances. Some categories, including health information and certain biometric information, receive extra protection as sensitive information.

The book’s Learner A–E records are invented for teaching. Replacing real names with labels would instead be pseudonymisation if people remain identifiable through a mapping or context. Removing names alone does not establish de-identification.

Before release, consider combinations, linkage and small groups. A public report about the only borrower of a rare item may identify that person even without a name. For this classroom project, use genuinely synthetic examples rather than a disguised real student register.

Reference: OAIC personal information explanation.

3. Know the Privacy Act and the course context

The federal Privacy Act 1988 governs personal-information handling by covered entities; the APPs are its principles-based framework. The syllabus requires the Privacy Act and APPs, but applicability depends on the organisation. Do not assume every Australian school falls under the same legislation.

OAIC explains that state/local government agencies, including public schools, are generally outside this federal Act. WA public-sector handling is subject to its own framework. A private school, service provider or other organisation needs its own coverage analysis.

WA context checked 15 October 2026: most substantive privacy provisions of the Privacy and Responsible Information Sharing Act 2024, including IPPs, commenced on 1 July 2026. Transitional rules differ by obligation and collection date. WA guidance states that the notifiable information breach provisions commence on 1 January 2027. This is separate from the federal APP framework and does not postpone internal incident reporting.

For an operational school decision, use current Department/school procedures and authorised privacy/records advice. Do not infer authority to disclose or dispose of records from a classroom APP exercise.

Sources: OAIC government-agency coverage and WA transition guidance. Recheck before reusing this dated legal-context note.

4. Apply selected APPs to design decisions

Course lensQuestion to askDesk decision
APP 1Make handling practices transparent.Provide an understandable policy and a way to raise concerns.
APP 3Justify necessary collection; sensitive information has additional rules.Do not add medical notes merely because a field is available.
APP 5Explain relevant collection details.Explain the purpose and relevant recipients at or before collection, or as soon as practicable afterwards if earlier notification is impracticable.
APP 6Limit use/disclosure to permitted purposes and exceptions.A loan register is not automatically a marketing list.
APP 8Consider obligations for overseas disclosure.Check a service and data flow before sending records offshore.
APP 10Take reasonable steps about information quality.Check a return status before relying on it.
APP 11Protect data; assess lawful retention and disposal.Restrict access and test backups; retention exceptions matter.
APPs 12–13Provide access/correction subject to applicable rules.Use an authorised request process rather than an informal public edit.

This is a selected study guide, not the full thirteen principles or their exceptions. Read the official APP text when checking a legal requirement. Consent is not a universal substitute for lawful purpose, appropriate collection or security.

APP 11 includes reasonable security steps. Its disposal/de-identification requirement has conditions and exceptions, including Commonwealth records and legally required retention. The WA records framework also imposes retention/disposal requirements. Do not translate “minimise retention” into “delete everything”.

Source: WA State Records Office privacy and recordkeeping guidance.

5. Follow the data through its lifecycle

Follow one loan record from collection to disposal. Where does it go, who can access it, and what copies are created? This sequence is its data lifecycle:

collection → storage → use → disclosure → retention/disposal

Include exports, screenshots, backups and external tools. Protecting only the original database file leaves the other copies out of your review.

StageDecision and evidence
CollectionRecord purpose and why each field is needed; use synthetic classroom data.
StorageList who can read/change files; protect copies and credentials.
UseState allowed tasks and check records before decisions.
DisclosureVerify recipient, purpose, authority and approved channel/service.
Retention/disposalRecord the applicable approved schedule/process, including copies and exceptions.
Access/correctionExplain how requests are routed and how changes preserve accountability.

A backup is another copy requiring access and retention controls. An overseas service question requires examining the actual data flow and applicable obligations, not assuming a product name proves where data is handled.

6. Work through a disclosure decision

The desk wants to publish a screenshot showing that its overdue report works. It contains borrower identifiers and exact dates. Known: the report can demonstrate the query. Risk: the audience may identify real borrowers or treat a false status as fact.

For the textbook/class demo, regenerate the report using invented records. Keep evidence of the query and expected outputs while avoiding real personal information. Before any operational release, check purpose, audience, identifiability, authority and applicable policy. Encryption of the upload would protect transport but would not authorise the disclosure.

A strong answer explains the benefit, affected people, evidence and less intrusive alternative. It does not claim that deleting one name column automatically makes the export safe.

Visual walkthrough

Check before sharing a loan screenshot

The report can demonstrate a working query without exposing real borrower records.

Pause and predict: Why is deleting the name column insufficient on its own?

Show the explanation

Other details or a separate mapping can still identify people. Removing names alone does not establish de-identification.

Try a small change: Explain how a synthetic screenshot can demonstrate the query while avoiding real borrower disclosure.

7. Explain ethical hacking and penetration testing

Ethical security testing aims to find and reduce weaknesses within valid authorisation. Penetration testing uses agreed techniques to examine whether weaknesses can be exploited and what the impact would be, then reports findings for remediation. It is not permission to explore every reachable system.

Before any testing, agree on the boundaries with someone who has authority over the system:

  • Which systems and data may you test?
  • Which methods are allowed, and at what times?
  • When must you stop, whom must you contact, and how must you handle evidence?

These boundaries are the scope. A classmate’s permission is not the responsible owner’s authority. A third-party system needs its own applicable authorisation.

Unauthorised access or activity outside agreed scope can be unethical and unlawful even if intended to help. If an unexpected issue falls outside scope, stop that line of testing and report through the agreed route. Testing results are limited to scope/time; passing does not prove that no vulnerability exists.

Reference: ASD security-assurance guidance.

8. Practice an authorisation review

Use the downloadable scope exercise: a teacher-owned local training app, invented borrower records, read-only review of provided configuration and logs, and checks using supplied accounts. Production systems, other students’ devices, real credentials and disruptive techniques are excluded. The document is a discussion exercise, not an actual permission grant.

Decide whether each proposed action is within that scope. Explain the authority and condition, not merely whether the action sounds useful. Scanning the production portal is outside scope; reviewing a supplied training log is within scope. Publishing the log externally needs separate disclosure authority.

A report should record scope, evidence, impact, limitations and recommended remediation without collecting more information than needed. Follow the owner’s reporting route rather than publicly exposing a weakness or identifying affected people.

9. Evaluate the database with evidence

Return to one acceptance criterion at a time:

  1. State what the database should do.
  2. Find evidence, such as a query result, test log, schema comparison or recovery check.
  3. Decide whether the criterion is met, partly met or not met.
  4. Explain a limitation and a realistic improvement.

For example, a successful joined report supports a reporting criterion. It does not prove that access controls or recovery also work.

CriterionEvidence to inspectPossible limitation
ReportsJoined outputs and expected rows/order.Unmatched borrowers are omitted by an inner join.
Data changesTargeted before/after records and rollback check.Calendar-date/overlap rules are not enforced by the starter.
AccessActual file/application access test in the authorised environment.A visual login alone does not protect the database file.
RecoveryA separate restored copy passes baseline checks.Restoration may lose recent changes and does not undo disclosure.
PrivacyField-purpose decisions and synthetic demonstration files.A deployment using real data requires further authorised review.

Do not present proposed controls as implemented. A rejected negative cost demonstrates that constraint, not factual accuracy of every cost. The existence of a backup file does not prove that recovery works; test a suitable restoration before relying on it.

11. Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence

Use the cases below as starting points, not a complete test plan. Write the expected outcome before running code, issuing SQL or revealing the explanation. For a conceptual claim, use the scenario and a counterexample; for implemented behaviour, record observed results. If the school has not run a check, label it pending.

Pause and predict

Choose one row and justify the expected outcome without using the program's output as your answer key.

Choose a case and predict first

  • Report can use fictional records
  • Proposed public dataset includes personal identifiers
Show expected evidence and why each case matters
Input / scenarioExpected evidenceWhy this case?
Report can use fictional recordsDo not collect real names unnecessarilyData minimisation in the exercise
Proposed public dataset includes personal identifiersApply approved review/de-identification before releaseSharing needs a purpose and controls

Build understanding in steps

  1. Guided completion: Complete the first case with teacher modelling, the second with a partner, then swap explanations and challenge one assumption.
  2. Independent transfer: Create a third case that could expose an error the first two would miss. Record the expected and actual evidence, explain any mismatch, repair one cause and repeat both the new case and earlier cases.
  3. Delayed retrieval: Return after another topic and attempt a changed case without viewing the worked explanation. Explain what transferred and what still needs support.

Original ungraded teaching addition · 30 October 2026. Download examples and activity pack · Teacher guidance

Practice and explain

Distinguish

Does replacing real names with B001–B004 guarantee de-identification?

Show explained answer

No. A mapping or other context may identify people. These book records are invented; relabelling actual records is a different process.

Apply

Does an encrypted transfer authorise sharing the loan register?

Show explained answer

No. Transport security and permission to disclose are separate decisions. Check purpose, recipients, authority and applicable rules.

Qualify

Should all school records be deleted immediately after the project?

Show explained answer

No. Check authorised retention/disposal requirements and exceptions. Minimise unnecessary copies without destroying records that must be retained.

Scope

Does a classmate’s approval authorise testing the school portal?

Show explained answer

No. Establish authority from the responsible owner and an agreed scope. The classroom scope exercise concerns a local training system only.

Evaluate

Can a successful negative-cost test prove the whole database is secure?

Show explained answer

No. It demonstrates one constraint. Access, data quality, recovery and privacy need separate evidence.

Your practical task

Analyse four decision scenarios, review the testing scope and complete the privacy/evaluation template. Demonstrate the database against its criteria, including actual report/change/recovery evidence. Explain one unimplemented control and one realistic improvement.

Show illustrative answer / example

Use evidence and context: unnecessary sensitive fields need justification; coded IDs may still identify; disclosures require authority; testing must stay within valid scope; retention follows applicable rules. Evaluate each criterion separately and label controls implemented, tested or proposed. Use synthetic files for classroom sharing.

Check your understanding

Which evidence best supports the claim that the database recovery process works?

A backup file exists A separate restored copy passes the planned record and query checks The report says backups are important

Quick-check answer and explanation

A separate restored copy passes the planned record and query checks

A checked restoration demonstrates recovery in the tested conditions. File existence or a proposed policy alone does not.

Chapter recap

Start with the purpose of collecting information. Check identifiability, authorised use, protection, correction and retention. Security testing needs valid authority and a clear scope. When evaluating your database, separate what you have implemented and tested from what you only propose.

Suggested classroom sequence
  1. Lesson 1: privacy/security/ethics/law; personal information; selected APP and WA-context scenarios.
  2. Lesson 2: ethical hacking and penetration-test scope; evidence/disclosure/retention decisions and feedback.
  3. Lesson 3: project evaluation workshop; match acceptance criteria to report, constraint, recovery and privacy evidence.
  4. Lesson 4: project self-review; explain limitations and prioritise improvements.

1. Data-quality clinic

Before changing a suspicious value, decide what needs checking:

  • Currency: is the evidence up to date?
  • Authenticity: is its source genuine?
  • Relevance: does it serve the purpose?
  • Accuracy: does it match reality?
  • Outliers: does an unusual value need investigation?

An extreme value may be correct. Preserve the source and record any authorised correction rather than deleting it just because it looks unusual.

Task A in the workbook supplies an old status, a valid but wrong date, an unverified message, unrelated health notes and an extreme cost. Explain a verification action and justified outcome for each.

2. Read a six-table extension

Work through the diagram in a fixed order:

  1. Locate the primary keys (PKs) and foreign keys (FKs).
  2. Read each relationship in both directions, including its minimum and maximum participation.
  3. Start at a Loan record and follow its references through Equipment to Category and Supplier.
  4. Compare it with the earlier four-table diagram. Identify which two tables are new.

Check the support booklet’s notation before drawing your own model.

3. Create and reconcile a fresh model

Use the workbook rules to model Member, Activity, Leader and Participation. Participation records the link between a member, an activity and a term. Use that three-part key, then document its fields.

Compare this with an optional one-to-one locker allocation. A foreign key alone allows repeated references; an appropriate uniqueness rule is also needed to limit the relationship to one-to-one.

Now compare your conceptual data dictionary with the actual starter SQL. Look for these differences:

  • CategoryName is not UNIQUE.
  • TEXT alone does not enforce the specified lengths or identifier patterns.
  • Returned has no DEFAULT, despite the earlier conceptual rule.

For each difference, record the intended rule and what the code actually enforces. Then justify a constraint or a change to the documentation. Calendar dates and overlapping loans still need separate checks.

Visual walkthrough

Planned rule versus actual constraint

A data dictionary describes the intended design. Inspect the SQL before claiming that each rule is enforced.

Pause and predict: Does NOT NULL on CategoryName prevent two categories having the same name?

Show the explanation

No. NOT NULL prevents a missing value. A separate uniqueness rule is needed to prevent repeated names.

Try a small change: Explain a test you could use to check whether an identifier-pattern rule is enforced.

1. Diagnose without the answer key

Without checking the answers, explain a key and its reference, 2NF versus 3NF, an inner join, CIA and AAA, authentication factors, a cipher, and a privacy or testing boundary.

Notice where you hesitate or can name a term without explaining it. Turn that gap into a question: “Why does an inner join leave out a borrower with no loans?”

Use your question to choose practice. Afterwards, answer it again without looking at the explanation.

2. Work through targeted stations

Choose two stations that match the gaps you identified:

  • Modelling: normalise a fresh club register.
  • SQL: find a row-count trap and practice a controlled change with rollback.
  • Security: explain a control and a situation it does not cover.
  • Ciphers and responsible data: trace a cipher, then explain a data-quality or privacy decision.

Use the earlier workbooks. Afterwards, explain what you corrected and why the new answer works.

Visual walkthrough

Turn a gap into useful practice

Choose practice that addresses a question you cannot yet explain.

Pause and predict: Would an unused equipment item appear in an inner-join loan-history report?

Show the explanation

No. Without a matching Loan row, that equipment item is omitted from this inner join.

Try a small change: Explain the same rule without using table names from the equipment-desk project.

3. Retest with changed circumstances

Try a new example before deciding that a gap is fixed. Explain each situation:

  • A borrower with no loans is omitted from an inner-join loan report.
  • Two cameras share a description.
  • A returned loan has an early due date.
  • A valid-looking date is factually wrong.
  • A suspicious message has not been clicked.

Identify the relevant rule or evidence before changing the model or query, or claiming that an incident occurred.

1. Use the original practice paper

Download student paper Explained answers

The paper has sixteen original practice questions. You can try it in 80 minutes or split it into two 40-minute halves over two lessons.

Use it as an optional learning activity, with explained answers for self-review. Every question starts with the original project data, so a change in one answer does not carry into the next question.

2. Bring the specified stimulus

Keep the supplied schema, loan rows and fictional costs beside you. In the SQL data, Returned uses 0/1 and dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

For Q4, use the separate six-table conceptual diagram. Supplier and Inspection are part of that diagram, but they are not tables in the project starter. Read the question’s supplied model before choosing which tables to discuss.

Diagram for Q4 · Project database for checking after the attempt

3. Check, correct and explain limits

After you try a question, use the separate guide to check your reasoning:

  1. Compare the rule, query or explanation, allowing equivalent accurate answers.
  2. Identify what was missing or incorrect. Focus on why each point matters.
  3. Rewrite the answer using the rule and the evidence.
  4. Try an example with changed data to see whether the correction transfers.

The paper checks a sample of theory and written SQL. You still need hands-on practice to draw ER models, create a database, test it and demonstrate recovery.

The suggested teaching sequence reserves weeks 17–18 for the school’s exam period. It adds no new teaching or project deadlines.
